quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

author: fundstrat
quoted_text:
Two major pieces of Ethereum news landed today: Deutsche Bank, Germany’s largest bank, is reportedly preparing to offer institutional ETH custody, while JPMorgan, the largest bank in the United States, is bringing JPM Coin’s tokenized dollar deposits to Ethereum.

Two giants of traditional finance embracing Ethereum and ETH. But the price barely reacted, whereas on another network, people would be expecting a major pump.

There are two reasons for this. 

First, ETH is larger and more liquid than most competing assets, so it takes more buying pressure to move it. Second, the market already expects major institutions to build on Ethereum. Another announcement is not subverting expectations.

Some people might say Ethereum is cursed: success is expected, and it only has something to lose when it disappoints.

This is where Ethereum bulls diverge from bears.

For years, bulls predicted the adoption now materializing before our eyes. This was NOT consensus. People said institutions would never use Ethereum, or would build everything privately.

Now it’s: “That’s already priced in. Good for Ethereum, but how does it accrue value to ETH?”

There are two things that mentality ignores.

First, this is financial adoption, with size. The players matter, but so do the capital they commit, the assets they tokenize, and how deeply they integrate their products and services.

All of that shows growing trust in Ethereum as a financial network, both for people using layer one directly and for layer twos using it for settlement.

We are gradually building an internet of finance where the underlying network has one native asset: Ether.

ETH secures that system and can be used directly as collateral. Bringing Bitcoin or any other asset, into Ethereum requires additional backing, bridge, or custody arrangements. Native ETH already belongs there.

Why does this matter so much?
Financial activity settling on Ethereum does not pay Bitcoin’s miners. Bitcoin’s own security model anticipates transaction fees replacing its declining issuance. That activity will not magically show up on Bitcoin just because its proponents expect it to.

Second, the uncertainty pushed around ETH’s supply ignores what has actually happened.

Since the Merge, ETH’s net supply has grown roughly 1.3% in total, while continuing to reward the stakers securing it. Stakers can earn above supply dilution, with transaction income on top. For an asset used as a store of value, that cannot simply be ignored.

There is already actual substance behind ETH’s gradual recognition as a store of value. The network has matured. Proof of stake has years of operation behind it. Current SEC guidance identifies ETH as a digital commodity. The ETFs that critics said would never happen now exist, including BlackRock’s multibillion-dollar fund.

Treasury companies like Bitmine and Sharplink are accumulating ETH at scale, and their holdings can produce staking income. That adds another way for investors to gain exposure, and another reason to hold the asset.

So when bulls talk about ETH eventually flipping Bitcoin, then gold, this is what they are looking at: an asset with restrained supply growth, native yield, and direct usefulness in a growing financial system.

You can disagree with that thesis. But “the price didn’t move” does not answer it. Fundamentals are moving int the right direction, but price is a lagging metric.

Many of the things bulls expected are happening. The argument is that ETH is severely underpriced, and that the market still underestimates where it leads.

author: donnoh_eth
quoted_text:
I made a visualization of EIP-8288 aka "recursive mempool aggregation," my new favorite EIP of all time because it perfectly encapsulates the thesis of the "cryptographic world computer" -- a system whose scalability *increases*, not decreases, with the level of decentralization.

In a previous tweet I explained how EIP-8288 achieved this seemingly impossible feat, but one gif is worth a thousand words.

Essentially, EIP-8288 leverages Ethereum's decentralized mempool as a parallel ZK proving cluster.  Clients send signatures and proofs to the mempool, which over multiple rounds progressively aggregate them into fewer and fewer proofs, until the block builder finally aggregates them into one SINGLE proof.

This design accomplishes five things at once:

- The more nodes we add to the decentralized mempool, the more signatures/proofs Ethereum can process as a whole.  This is obvious if you look at the animation and imagine more nodes in the mempool ring, which would "fan out" to more signatures/proofs.

- By aggregating over multiple rounds (aka "recursive aggregation"), the bandwidth consumed by proofs remains constant for each node even as the network processes more proofs.  As a result, the network stays decentralized even as capacity increases.

- By aggregating proofs before one final aggregation by the builder, as opposed to requiring the builder to aggregate everything, the network can process more proofs without increasing hardware requirements for the builder.

- By aggregating everything to a single block-level proof, validators can verify thousands of signatures/proofs by checking just one aggregated proof.  Hardware requirements for validators can therefore stay low, keeping the network decentralized.

- By aggregating not just native signatures but also STARKs, Ethereum can support any signature scheme by wrapping them in STARKs.

So once again, this is how Ethereum will:

- scale to process tens of thousands of PQ and private transactions per second

- charge a tiny amount of gas to validate each txn, even though the original signature/proof may be huge (up to hundreds of KBs in size)

- all while decentralizing even MORE.

You are not bullish enough.

Until now, the only known Korean suppliers were HPSP and Hanmi Semiconductor.

Now TheElec reports that Tesla and SpaceX are in talks across nearly every category Korean companies can supply, from basic piping parts to process materials to test components.

At SEMICON West in San Francisco last week, Terafab staff walked straight to around 10 Korean booths on the morning of day one, including ENF Technology, Dongjin Semichem, Hanmi Semiconductor, Unisem and MiCo.

Several companies have already signed NDAs. One got an NDA by email the same evening Terafab visited its booth.

Hanmi Semiconductor is discussing TC bonders for Terafab, and HPSP has agreed to supply one high pressure hydrogen annealing tool to the R&D line.

MiCo's cleaning unit Komico signed a three way NDA with Tesla and SpaceX about a month ago, and ISC is already swapping samples for rubber test sockets.

Tesla and SpaceX do not buy from Chinese suppliers. One Korean supplier put it simply, without China there are only a few options, and Japan is expensive.

They also want prices that are CHEAPER than China.

$LRCX and $AMAT have reportedly built dedicated Terafab teams, and Fujifilm is meeting Terafab buyers regularly on slurries, photoresist and etchants.

The goal is a fab with 1 million wafer starts per month within 10 years, with $16.8 billion of initial investment and more than 3,000 jobs.

SpaceX broke ground in Grimes County, Texas this month, and the first 100,000 wafer per month phase is expected before 2030.

Logic is being done with $INTC, talks with $TSM are ongoing, and memory will be built separately.

One supplier said that if they email Terafab in the middle of the night in the United States, they get an answer in 30 minutes to an hour.

$TSLA and $SPCX are building a chip supply chain at Elon speed.

author: OAK_Res_FR
quoted_text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

I WAS BUILDING A HOUSE!

I commute to work. I’ve done so for decades. It has become somewhat cathartic. I listen to audiobooks on Audible, podcasts, and music. I practice singing and even worship during my commute. Sometimes I just think. It’s a rural path for the most part but I remain alert for wildlife that may be interested in commuter-assisted suicide. Humans with intent to kill me with their vehicles only become a factor during the last few miles as I approach my office.

My work grants me the privilege of a company vehicle which I usually drive for my commutes. Now and then I drive my personal car. A modified 2019 Volkswagen GTI. It’s low, fast, and loud. Custom exhaust, race clutch, upgraded intercooler, aftermarket wheels and suspension, ECU Stage 2 tune—all the things one does to these cars to improve them over stock, which is already pretty impressive. Anyway, it’s a fun car to drive and not so heavily modified that it’s impractical as a daily driver.

I drove it in today. Not fast. Just a normal, Gen-X driver listening to a podcast, navigating a path I’ve driven hundreds, maybe thousands of times at this point. Waiting at a stoplight, I turned my podcast down a bit. That’s a thing older men do, apparently. I was made aware of that recently by a younger person. We turn down our music or media when we’re in traffic or looking for an address so we can "see better." Whatever.

At the signal, I performed my standard left-and-right head swivel because I don’t trust anyone and it was still dark. As I straightened out after navigating the turn, the car that had been on my immediate left in the turning lane darted past, cut into my lane, and brake-checked me while simultaneously extending his left arm out the window to give me the universal sign inviting me to have relations with myself.

I had noticed the other car at the light. It had braked late and came to rest past the stop bar. The light from oncoming traffic across the intersection hit the side of the vehicle in such a way that I could see every imperfection in the paint. They were numerous. It appeared to have been painted with a brush. Flowers? I see flowers. Yes, flowers. As cars turned and more light flooded the "canvas," more detail was revealed. The base color was dark—either dark blue or black—and a wide, wavy pink or white stripe with rough borders encircled the entire car. In that stripe... wait, I get it! In that "ribbon" were hand-painted flowers. A Flower Power Ford Focus wagon. No hubcaps. The wheels were painted white. Okay.

I chuckled. Not about the car, necessarily. I laughed about Gene Hackman. Little Bill, more accurately. In the movie Unforgiven, Little Bill Daggett was a heinous human being, but he tried to paint himself otherwise. He didn’t try too hard, mind you, and he wasn’t very successful, but in his mind he was. That was clearly revealed when he delivered one of my favorite lines from the film. The moment he realized his end was certain, he uttered: "I don’t deserve this... to die like this. I was building a house."

So, did this driver of the flower-adorned Focus notice me studying his car and conclude that I had judged it to be lesser than my GTI? Had I somehow wronged him while we were traveling southbound on that other stretch of road before turning east? I don’t know, but I don’t think so. I’m a courteous and conscientious driver and not easily distracted. 

I will likely never know what inspired the thoughtful gesture, and while I appreciate the invitation to have relations with myself, I politely declined. I’ve been flipped off before. So what? The brake check was dumb, though. Sure, my car has new high-performance brakes with ABS and TCS, along with all the computer-aided, radar-assisted magic modern cars have, but the car behind me might have been a 1983 Buick. Those things need a zip code to stop.

Brake-checking another driver in traffic is a dumb thing to do, Little Bill.

text:
Therapy doesn’t work for me, and I’m not convinced it was built with autistic people in mind.

The second I walk into that room, I start masking on autopilot. It’s like my face has a “Customer Service Mode” button.

I can hear what she’s getting at beneath the words. I spot the technique. I can practically see the flowchart. So I leave feeling worse, not better: analysed, not helped.

To be fair, she’s doing her job. I get it. She’s trained to sound like she understands, warmly and thoughtfully, with the right pauses in the right places. But it feels like she’s performing empathy, not feeling it.

Meanwhile, I’m sat there thinking: Brilliant. I’ve just paid money to watch someone try to reverse-engineer my brain with a toolkit that doesn’t fit.

By the end, I’m the one doing the heavy lifting. I walk out knowing more about psychology than anything that actually helps with my daily struggles.

Anyone else feel the same?

author: carlosdomingo
quoted_text:
Jeff drank a bit too much of his own Kool-Aid in this recent Odd Lots clip. I think it's important to clear up a distinction that makes all the difference.

Democratizing access to wealth creation is NOT the same as democratizing access to speculation.

Many of us genuinely want broader participation in attractive investment opportunities. The growing wealth inequality produced by the current system is tearing at the seams of society, something I've spoken about many times.

But let's be clear: listing pre-IPO perpetual futures does absolutely nothing to democratize the wealth being created in private markets.

I've seen this misleading narrative pushed repeatedly by perp DEXs lately, and it needs to be called out.

A pre-IPO perp creates ZERO underlying wealth. It's a zero-sum contract before costs, and negative-sum after them. No capital flows to the company. No ownership changes hands. No new economic opportunity is created.

Every long has a short. There is no free lunch in simply going long something before its IPO, and funding costs can even determine the outcome more than any price moves. TRADING access is NOT INVESTING access.

In fact, in many ways pre-IPO perps are almost the antithesis of democratized access:

They create the illusion of participation in private-market wealth creation, while actually offering retail a speculative instrument whose mechanics they are often poorly equipped to understand.

The result is a playground for the FEW sophisticated traders who understand funding, oracle design, and liquidation mechanics to extract value from the MANY who don't.

To give credit where it's due, Robinhood's efforts toward sourcing actual employee shares, placing them into SPVs, and tokenizing genuine spot ownership are much closer to meaningful democratization.

That can unlock real economic value by allowing employees to exchange some of their expected upside for liquidity, while giving new investors actual economic exposure. A legitimate financial trade-off, without the funding-rate and liquidation shenanigans.

I'm strongly aligned with expanding access to investment opportunities. And I believe advances in AI and blockchain can dramatically lower the barriers to discovering, structuring, and distributing them.

But let's not BS ourselves that launching another zero-sum casino contract is moving the needle on wealth inequality.

What would actually move the needle is bringing real capital formation and ownership onchain. Giving investors access to productive, illiquid assets like data centers, GPUs, and select startup investing, where capital can actually finance growth and share in the resulting value creation.

These opportunities are harder to structure, underwrite, and bring to market, and we haven't seen many compelling implementations onchain yet. 

Hopefully this will change soon and, as the industry matures, we can direct more of our energy toward actually expanding access to wealth creation.

Clip below. Was glad to see @tracyalloway push back on this framing, and to Jeff's credit, after this he does seem to walk back his original position somewhat.

text:
A contract that pays for other people's transactions has one job. Say no to the wrong ones.

Most of them fail that job quietly, and the deposit is gone before anyone notices.

This is the sponsor pattern. A gas relayer, a fee manager, anything that pays, credits, or grants on behalf of someone else. Its entire economics live inside one validation check. Loosen that check and you built a faucet with extra steps.

Four ways it has broken in audits:

The permission got front-run. A binding step that enabled a policy and used it in the same call let an attacker race the mempool and attach that policy to a different identity.

The side door skipped the bouncer. One entry path enforced an account check. A second, less obvious path reached the same restricted state without it. Whatever your validator protects, count every door into it.

Anyone could write to the ledger. A fee-tracking function took a caller-supplied address and let anyone credit or debit it. Accounting that the public can write to is not accounting.

Removing one piece broke the gate. A validator quietly depended on a separate fallback module. Uninstall the fallback, and validation itself stopped working. Nobody had rehearsed that failure.

The rule: any function that spends, credits, or grants on someone's behalf must bind sender, target, and amount before it acts, and it must be checked against the exact same rules as its main entrance, every side path included.

If you cannot list what your sponsor logic binds before it says yes, that is the finding.

text:
I made a visualization of EIP-8288 aka "recursive mempool aggregation," my new favorite EIP of all time because it perfectly encapsulates the thesis of the "cryptographic world computer" -- a system whose scalability *increases*, not decreases, with the level of decentralization.

In a previous tweet I explained how EIP-8288 achieved this seemingly impossible feat, but one gif is worth a thousand words.

Essentially, EIP-8288 leverages Ethereum's decentralized mempool as a parallel ZK proving cluster.  Clients send signatures and proofs to the mempool, which over multiple rounds progressively aggregate them into fewer and fewer proofs, until the block builder finally aggregates them into one SINGLE proof.

This design accomplishes five things at once:

- The more nodes we add to the decentralized mempool, the more signatures/proofs Ethereum can process as a whole.  This is obvious if you look at the animation and imagine more nodes in the mempool ring, which would "fan out" to more signatures/proofs.

- By aggregating over multiple rounds (aka "recursive aggregation"), the bandwidth consumed by proofs remains constant for each node even as the network processes more proofs.  As a result, the network stays decentralized even as capacity increases.

- By aggregating proofs before one final aggregation by the builder, as opposed to requiring the builder to aggregate everything, the network can process more proofs without increasing hardware requirements for the builder.

- By aggregating everything to a single block-level proof, validators can verify thousands of signatures/proofs by checking just one aggregated proof.  Hardware requirements for validators can therefore stay low, keeping the network decentralized.

- By aggregating not just native signatures but also STARKs, Ethereum can support any signature scheme by wrapping them in STARKs.

So once again, this is how Ethereum will:

- scale to process tens of thousands of PQ and private transactions per second

- charge a tiny amount of gas to validate each txn, even though the original signature/proof may be huge (up to hundreds of KBs in size)

- all while decentralizing even MORE.

You are not bullish enough.
author: FigoETH
quoted_text:
Ultimately, precompiles and EVM are both the wrong place to put most cryptography support into Ethereum. The reason is that precompiles and EVM both operate on data that has to be included into the ethereum chain somehow, which realistically means included in a block as calldata. That space is limited - even with PeerDAS and blocks-in-blobs, there's a practical cap of ~8 MB/s before it starts getting uncomfortable.

Remember: it's not a blockchain. It's a cryptographic world computer. Any data/computation that does not need to be in the "main thread" of data/execution should not be put into the main thread.

Instead, the correct solution is... EIP-8288 maximalism.

If you have any heavy computation that's self-contained, compute it and STARK it client-side (this is quickly getting faster and faster, even on phones), and push the STARK through the EIP-8288 recursive aggregation mechanism. The chain sees the fact that the computation was done and what the result is; it never needs to see the actual data and computation.

This way everyone can use whatever cryptography they want, the Ethereum chain can be lean, and we never need to add more precompiles again.

text:
Over the last 30 days, Derive has remained over 90% of the onchain options market. In that same time frame, we’ve done about 5% of Deribit’s options volumes, up from 0.1% a year ago.

It’s difficult to build momentum in this category because of the uniquely strong network effects around options markets. Users and market makers hold positions and collateral on exchange for the duration of an option, often many months. The difficulty and cost of integration are a liquidity provider is an order of magnitude higher than perps. Options markets are also the last vertical to mature in any asset class.

Onchain has finally broken the dam - and Derive, alongside all of our builders and partners, has a chance to redefine the options category, first in crypto, and then beyond.

The tailwinds are enormous, and still underappreciated by most people I speak with.

1. Bringing options liquidity onchain unlocks more functionality than any other vertical: programmable, composable building blocks for precise, tailored yield generation, hedging, and speculative trades. One click hedges embedded in every brokerage and fintech, yield generation strategies with verifiable backtests and transparent risk, on any asset, new social trading experiences built using the kinds of trades only options can support.

2. AI for UX: the biggest barrier to entry to trading options is understanding. 2026 has seen a step function change in how models reason about options. This has yet to filter through to UX, but is coming. People shouldn’t trade options if they don’t understand them. But - given they want to express an opinion about the market - they should be able to find the best way to translate that into a trade. Options are often the best way to do so.

3. AI for agentic trading: options give you thousands of ways to express a view across strikes, expiries and structures. For many traders this is overwhelming, but for agents, it’s a much more useful set of choices. My wager is that agents will prefer specificity and precision when executing trades: not just whether an asset goes up or down, but how far, by when, and with how much risk. Options are the answer.

These tailwinds are strengthening just as our liquidity hits an inflection point. Big integrations take time to come to fruition, but we’re seeing the results month by month, with many more in the pipeline. At the same time, we’ve completed our biggest infrastructure upgrade in 3 years, taking what was already a leading onchain product into what I believe is the best options infrastructure anywhere.

We have so much more work to do, and will be constantly taking feedback, iterating on the product, and ensuring that every dollar of liquidity that onboards to Derive is earned. But we really are only at the dawn of the last major trading vertical to move onchain, and in my opinion, it will be the largest.

🧬 Virtual Embryo x Yukon 🧬

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.

quoted_text:
Was recently at a bar where drinks were dynamically priced, 

i.e. the more people bought a particular drink, the more expensive it became (price would then decayed over time towards a floor). 

Fascinating to watch a few market mechanisms play out in a bar: 

People ventured outside their usual orders in search of cheaper alternatives, often discovering new favorites in the process.

Others treated rising prices as signals of quality, happily paying premiums to try expensive drinks they’d never had before.

More experienced drinkers behaved like value investors, picking up underpriced drinks they already knew were good while everyone else chased the popular ones.

Price discovery, information leakage, herding, and utility trades all unfolded over rounds of drinks.

More bars should try this.

text:
Extraction models turn human language into data your software can act on. We're bringing them to Sage.

Early access tomorrow for everyone who registers on @levantolabs by 23:59 PT today.

Most software needs structured inputs. People communicate through emails, chats, tickets, contracts, and conversations.

Extraction models connect those two interfaces. You define the information your application needs, and the model identifies it in the text: people, companies, products, dates, amounts, descriptions, or requests.

Calling this “extracting stuff from documents” understates what developers can build with it.

Consider a customer message:

“The blue jacket arrived with a broken zip. Please send a replacement to 18 King Street.”

An extraction model can identify the product, defect, requested remedy, and address. Your application now has fields it can validate, look up, and pass to a tool.

A decision model can then evaluate whether the request qualifies for an automatic replacement, needs more information, or requires human review.

Extraction → decision → action.

Each stage has a defined responsibility. Extraction supplies the values. The decision model evaluates the available options against your policy and context. Your application validates the result and controls execution.

That separation matters for agent builders. You can inspect what the model extracted, test the decision independently, and control which actions are permitted.

Speed changes where this becomes useful.

At roughly 200 ms for extraction, developers can start putting language interpretation directly into interactive software:

• A support interface that fills relevant fields while an agent reads a ticket.
• A browser agent that extracts values from a message before populating a form.
• A find-in-page feature that highlights cancellation deadlines or product complaints, even when the text uses different wording.
• A workflow that turns an incoming email into validated tool arguments and evaluates the next action.

The opportunity extends to any application where someone currently reads a message, copies information into fields, and decides what happens next.

Developers can define the information they need and the decisions their software must make, then connect those outputs to existing functions.

We're bringing extraction and decision models together in Sage so builders can implement that flow.

Watch the demo below. Register on Levanto by 23:59 PT today for early access tomorrow.

text:
🇵🇱 Okay my final Poland video because we're leaving soon!

It was really fun and we had a great time

I liked Warsaw most to be honest, a very modern city, a bit like East Asia in terms of modernity, with rapid delivery services and apps, everything just works great and fast

I'm not saying it's perfect btw, there's moments where you still realize it's Eastern Europe (or as they'd like to call it Central Europe) but then the difference is they generally solve problems fast and pragmatically

Many shops you go will actually have a long line at the checkout, annoying, but usually there's a second checkout but it's closed

That's because Poland too has a big labor shortage, one of the lowest fertility rates in Europe, so they too kinda have to import people, but they choose to import them from Ukraine and Belarus (and some South Asians actually too)

But wait, so that checkout line is closed yes? I'm so used to Portugal where there is zero incentive to then open another checkout counter but in Poland usually within a few minutes they notice it's busy and open another counter. I know, basic stuff but hard to come by these days. They're fast and pragmatic

Ordering flowers for my gf was easy, the flower shop has an IG (but I don't) so I msg them over Whatsapp, they immediately respond, give me some options, I say what I want, address, payment link with Stripe (!) and done delivered at my hotel by a nice guy. All soooo smooth. Fast response, friendly people. Things just work here!

Poland has done a great job keeping bad immigrants out while bring good immigrants in. The Ukrainians and Belarussians are neighbors and their cultures overlap strongly with Poland. So they fit in easily. Same cultures, same religions, same routines etc. for the most part

A young Polish Uber driver I talked to said to him Krakow (his city) looks just like Lviv in Ukraine, so it's easy for Ukranians in Poland to integrate

There's a lot of police presence in places, and military vehicles also (probably cause of the Ukraine war), the security at the Warsaw Airport is not done by some 5 layer outsourced company with staff that hates you, but by friendly people from the Polish Border Guard (Straż Graniczna) wearing military uniforms

Warsaw has lots of skyscrapers now, and actually the tallest in Europe now at 310 meters is the Varso Tower, crazy!

Poland is a booming economy and growing fast. When you're growing of course it's easy to make things go well. I'd say it's important for Poland to look ahead carefully and don't make the same mistakes that Western Europe did when everything was going well and we were very rich

We became complacent, stagnant, added regulatory burdens, became overly obsessed with climate change and the environment, and imported the lowest quality tier of people from cultures that hate our guys and are diametrically opposed to Western culture

That last part is especially interesting considering Poland's history, where 6 million (!) or 20% of the country was ruthlessly murdered in World War II

I think that gives them the power to not have to be politically correct about immigration like Germany, because Poland after all was the victim, while Germany then was the purpetreyor. Which is why Germany does have to be so politically correct about it, due to extreme historical guilt

You walk on the streets of Poland in the day and at night and you see the difference what sane policy does to daily life

We're all dealing with the echoes of history

So my message to my Polish friends: don't make the same mistakes Western Europe did and you will soon be the richest, safest, most modern country in Europe and hopefully then have the power to be the new leader of Europe

And maybe you can then save Europe as a whole!!

Niech żyje Polska! 🇵🇱

text:
Tulip is treating every dollar @Aave DAO spends as value extraction while ignoring what the DAO gets in return.

1. Aave Will Win Framework: The proposal expands the DAO's revenue sources by directing all Aave-branded product revenue towards it (directly related to point 4).

Before then, there was a $50M annual buyback framework, proposed when Aave's annualized revenue based on 30d performance was ~$204M (about 25% of revenue).

At today's ~$108M, the same fixed buyback would be ~46%, as a large share of that revenue came from LRT looping that unwound after the Kelp/LZ exploit.

The $50M buyback allo had no programmatic link with protocol revenue, nor an equivalent mechanism to the one proposed by the Aave Will Win framework to ensure that revenue from Aave's growing product suite accrued to the DAO.

The only reason why any token holder would oppose such a proposal is due to (a) spite or (b) wanting a better framework. However, (b) can be addressed later without wasting more time delaying a revenue distribution framework.

2. Pause AAVE buybacks: This was proposed by TokenLogic, not Aave Labs, and it was a good decision given the circumstances. The DAO used to have service providers who didn't perform proper due diligence on the assets they listed, specifically rsETH.

Once LayerZero was hacked, $AAVE token holders paid the price. Aave faced ~$124M in estimated bad debt under one scenario, with another reaching $230M. That's roughly 2.5 years of buybacks. In order to rebuild Aave's balance sheet, TokenLogic proposed to pause buybacks.

Also, if you look at the vast majority of successful organizations, they don't prioritize buybacks when they can put that capital toward growing the business. Aave is (a) rebuilding its balance sheet and (b) prioritizing growth efforts.

3. No rush to restart buybacks: The above paragraph applies here as well. Additionally, the Aave App could become Aave's largest distribution channel by orders of magnitude. Combine it with stable vaults and we can see an absurd number of financial institutions and fintechs using Aave in the back. In other words, Aave App can bring users and capital into Aave, while third-party fintech integrations could expand distribution further.

Shipping Aave App and scaling it is +EV for the DAO, grants considered. At a ~13–14% take rate, the App needs to generate ~$36–38M in fees for the DAO to recoup the $5M bonus. If it becomes even a fraction of the distribution channel it could be, that's an easy bar.

4. The Aave Foundation: This initiative aims to formalize the DAO's ownership of the Aave IP. This matters because the Aave Will Win framework directs Aave-branded revenue to the DAO, and the Foundation is what gives the DAO legal ownership of that brand.

Cayman was chosen because a foundation company under the Cayman Foundation Companies Act can exist without members or shareholders while still holding legal title, executing contracts, and appearing in court. That is what makes it possible to own the trademark and defend it without creating an owner who sits above the DAO.

Tulip King is a gigabrain, but bad blood prevents a lot of very smart individuals from seeing how Aave is positioning itself to scale, succeed and benefit token holders. Truth is, even in rebuild mode, Aave trades at ~33x FDV/revenue. Kamino is at ~50x, Morpho generates no revenue at all.

text:
🧬 Virtual Embryo x Yukon 🧬

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.

text:
「 曾经加密货币行业 Saylor 级别的人物，如今精神失常，滥用药物、枪支 」

Ben Armstrong 曾是加密货币世界中最具影响力的人物之一。以 BitBoy 的身份闻名，他的 YouTube 频道拥有 150 万订阅者

他说自己从 2012 年就开始购买比特币。有兰博基尼，有声称价值数千万美元的财富，每天有成千上万的人观看他提供“消息”和项目推荐

粉丝对他的共识是 “跟着 BitBoy，就能致富”，但现在一切都逐渐崩塌

- 2023 年 8 月

他被自己公司解雇。他的合伙人称存在药物滥用问题、对员工造成伤害，以及资金管理问题。他亲手打造的频道仍由公司掌控，然后被改名为 Discover Crypto。BitBoy 失去了让他成名的品牌

但事情并未就此结束

他的妻子提出离婚，原因是有外遇。他曾私自在合伙人的房子里直播，大发雷霆的抱怨自己兰博基尼被偷了。随后警察来了，在他车上发相枪支与药物，而那辆豪车最终也没有下落

曾经拥有的数千万财富耗尽了，由于各种控诉，每月律师费高达 10 万美元

- 2025 年 3 月

各种状况变得更加严重

他在佛罗里达被捕。指控是：向佐治亚州的一名法官发送被视为威胁的电子邮件。他面临重罪指控，可能判处 5–10 年监禁。几个月后，他又因一起被视为骚扰的电话案再次被捕

- 2026 年 2 月

他指控 Kevin O’Leary 涉嫌 2019 年一起船只事故相关的谋杀，甚至散布了他的私人电话号码。结果，联邦法院对他下达了价值 280 万美元的默认判决

从加密货币界最大的影响者，到如今生活充斥着法律纠纷、债务和声誉崩塌

- 加密货币世界提供了获取功名利禄的机会，同时也会不断挑逗你人性中最邪恶的部分

- 从 Nobody 到成名很快，从人生赢家跌入深渊更快

text:
我的经验，通常像 Claude 这样前沿模型，你不指定它默认就是这一套东西，已经被训练的够够的，完全不需要太刻意提示。

反而因为 AI 喜欢用 shadcn/ui，做出来都一个样，看的人审美疲劳。

所以 Claude Design 在设计的时候，它为了不做出来千篇一律，特别强调设计系统在其中的作用，引导你去先导入也好制作也好搞一套设计系统（Design System）出来，然后你做 PPT、做网页、甚至做视频，都用这一套设计系统，那么你的风格就会和设计系统保持一致，不会出现千篇一律的 AI 默认风格。

即使你不用 Claude Design，这种先引入设计系统的方式也是可以借鉴的，可以避免你做出来的网页风格大众化，而且可以很好的保证风格的一致性。

而且有很多开源开放的设计系统可以选，比如我直接用的 Adobe 的设计系统，做出来的东西至少不算难看。

text:
Paper 项目方赚麻了，不仅第一时间生息回本，现在连规则都改了。说得好听是“项目转型”，说得难听就是“欺骗+软 rug” 啦。具体内容总结如下：
1. $Paper 代币短期不会开放交易。
币卖不得了！同步 Hyperliquid 上的 Paper 代币合约也立即被撤下。
社区预期是：会在几周内开放转账并上线 DEX。
但现在：团队明确说不会开放交易——并且没有开放交易的计划路线图。
也就是说之前所有的预期——不论是财库、Meme 还是撸空投，全都归零！

2.短线费用增加，量化机器人失去生存空间。
项目方将一开始上线时的 0.2 个基点小额费用调整为额外收费（实测为 15 倍费率以上），基本打穿了之前网上流传的一些量化套利策略。
公告中还明确指出：后续会进行进一步调整费率——也就是说团队会根据量化薅羊毛的情况，进一步提高费用。
另一方面，项目团队能够分得的手续费就更多了。

3. 代币铸造规则改了，老持有者会被慢慢稀释。
之前是按照铸造曲线进行亏损铸造，但现在项目方从绝对数量改成供应量的固定比例。
新规则：每亏 100 万美元铸造当时供应量的约 0.1%。

- 早期大户：所占据的份额会随着时间不断稀释，越后进的用户越容易拿到较多的份额。
- 新用户：不管什么时候进来，亏 100 万大约买到全体 PAPER 的 0.1%。

所有权的价格固定了，早进晚进没有区别，区别只在于你的份额之后会被持续稀释。

你越晚进，拿到的绝对数量就会越多！

当然，平台还对一些协议接口和平台的边缘计算进行了一点优化，用来防止破产攻击。

总结来说：
1. 平台定位由撸毛挖矿变为交易平台。
平台在宣发时暗示的挖矿和空投全部取消，转而鼓励真实交易，并提高了本身手续费的收益。
已经能看到平台的转型路线：逐渐建设一个真实的交易平台，而不是亏损挖矿的撸毛协议。
这对协议长期健康是对的，因为激励的是持续交易，而不是一次性刷币后躺着分红，所以会吸引更多的交易员前来，平台确实也对此提高了手续费。
这次变动的代价是：早期参与者的预期被改写了，或者说，他们被割惨了！

2. $PAPER 的定位从股权改成了返佣。
旧曲线下，早期亏损者拿到的是一份基本不会被稀释的未来现金流权利；新曲线下，所有人的份额都按指数衰减，只有持续交易才能维持份额。
亏损后的代币质押分红完全无法覆盖亏损本身，所以亏损代币分红的定位已经不是资产，而是对交易手续费的弥补。
在这个程度上，$PAPER 更像返佣（以分红的形式），而非代币与股权。

3. 平台最大的风险为项目方作恶风险，随意调整规则，使得项目方可以随意操纵平台和调整预社区期。
之前我在帖子https://t.co/op4M2kmtGZ 里面提到过：项目方仍对平台协议具有完全主导权，以协议升级为理由可以随意更改费率与平台规则。

目前看来，这个担忧成为了现实。
今天项目方可以把平台的定位由撸毛挖矿改为交易平台，那么明天、后天的手续费与代币经济学调整，仍可能又一次出乎所有人意料。

甚至有一种可能：这是项目方在故意为之的一次 FUD。
也就是说存在这样一种可能：项目方可能想收集筹码+发币的预期的目的，所以故意通过制造 FUD 进行新的筹码收集，在收集到足够筹码之后，再完成代币转换、代币转账和上币交易。

我们对此无法预料，但这其实能看出：当平台的规则完全掌握在项目方手里，社区没有任何力量与之抗衡。
author: xizhe_chan
quoted_text:
A note on transferability.

Papertrade is a complicated primitive, and managing it from a risk standpoint is a complicated problem. The PAPER token is far more integrated into the economics of the primitive than most tokens are in their respective protocols today, and, broadly, was designed to act as a counter insolvency incentive coupled with a rebate mechanism to losing traders. Market makers and exchanges are by far the two most profitable businesses in crypto, and our goal was to try and externalise as much of their margins back to users as possible. We are now just over a week into the life of papertrade and we are becoming increasingly confident that this is both possible, but also a likely outcome as agentic led software becomes the norm. 

As it stands, the paper token traded as a perp becomes a leveraged bet on bankroll solvency - and being able to short bankroll solvency materially changes the payoff curve of a manipulation attack. The target number goes from the bankroll, to the bankroll + short side exposure on paper. We can, and do limit bankroll size specifically to control this payoff curve and ensure it never becomes existentially problematic, but external perp markets are not something we would have any control over if left to float of their own accord. For example, if our bankroll is $10m, an attack costing $15m manipulating the price of bitcoin or ether is not viable. You simply lose money. If however you were also able to put on $10m of PAPER short side exposure, suddenly an attack costing $15m is very viable indeed.

If we were to make the token transferable at this point, we are confident we would quickly enter a state too dangerous to allow any material exposure to be taken on papertrade, an end result that benefits no party beyond the wolves who have done the math on the short and are waiting in the wings with sharpened knives.

We would also like to thank the various perps teams who have reached out about pre-market listings for their understanding and patience regarding this issue, and especially to the paragon team who, despite jumping the gun on us, have behaved with the utmost integrity and transparency once a dialogue was opened.

Perps on PAPER will always act as a self-limiting exposure ceiling for a token with this type of utility, and we think it would be a shame to limit the growth of papertrade to the extent that allowing perps would necessitate. As such, at this juncture we do not have plans to allow off-contract token transferability.

Structurally, papertrade is limited by the quality of the data it receives from hyperliquid, but we strongly believe that hyperliquid has a very large part to play in the future of global exchanges, and expect their books to continue to thicken and strengthen over time.

A note on fees.

Papertrade launched with a deadband fee from entry of 0.2bps. This means you don't earn anything until the price has moved by 0.002% in your favour. Over the months before launch, we played around with many different curves and fee structures affecting exclusively positions closed very close to entry price in order to try and devise a structure that removed the edge against the bankroll low time frame scalp bots have, whilst also minimally impacting the traders around which and for whom the product was devised. We were never able to find anything we were absolutely happy with and so decided to stay with the 0.2bp deadband fee through launch. This has however meant we have had to be very restrictive when it came to certain parameters, such as OI caps.

Now, however, we have enough live data to fully understand exactly which strategies work, and to make the necessary changes to stop them. The changes we are making will have an on hours and off hours fee mode to account for the relative differences in liquidity the hyperliquid books see between these two time periods, and the ease with which low time frame moves are signalled. The changes we are making will only affect positions closed within 6bps of entry (0.06%) in on hours, and 10bps (0.1%) in off hours. Any trades closed above these threshold price shifts will see no change to their fees at all. On a look back to launch basis, these changes affect the profitability of bot strategies roughly 15x more than they do normal traders, for whom a very small proportion of overall winnings come from within this band.

These changes should serve to flatten much of the edge our microfee structure necessarily creates on low time frames, and will help with long term exchange sustainability. This should hopefully allow us to open up parameters such as OI caps a little more so those of you who wish to can put on the size you want to, when you want to.

It is possible these changes are still too lax, and that further revisions to this structure may be necessary going forwards. If so, we will notify users ahead of time.

A note on paper tokenomics. 

In conjunction with the fee changes, we will also be implementing a change to the token issuance curve.

Going forward, every $1 lost mints a fixed share of PAPER's supply at that moment, roughly 0.1% of supply per $1M lost (the exact number depends on the mint rate at the time the contracts are upgraded). PAPER minting in and near insolvency will also change, switching from a flat 100 per $1 of loss, to a time weighted multiplier on the curve growing over time, effectively acting as the house running a discounted auction on its own future cash flows. This change also removes the risk of the paper-mint-straddle-attack, temporarily pushing the protocol insolvent by closing only the winning side of a large straddle position and then attempting to mint as much paper as possible. 

In the immediate term these changes will only have a very subtle effect on PAPER minting, but in the long run will structurally change the outlook of the system beyond the first few weeks, serving to slowly dilute out older holders and leaving more recent users with an advantage. Reconstituting the PAPER system into something much closer to the exchange rakeback it was intended to be.

We have been very reticent to touch this particular aspect of the system for obvious reasons, but ultimately we believe that these changes provide all users with the optionality to take a smaller piece of a potentially much larger pie than the current dynamic might necessarily allow.

Other, miscellaneous notes.

These contract upgrades will include a few other contract changes, including the addition of builder codes so that builders can utilise papertrade in whatever capacity they choose to. This will be a whitelist only to begin with and we will have more for you later in the week on where/how this will be rolled out. A small change to contract permissions on the reward distributor and a change on how below bust closes are processed by the exchange are also included, largely to block gas griefing attacks. 

These changes will be pushed to docs in full over the coming day, and we will further announce once the changes are queued into the timelock pending final security passes, scheduled to go live 24 hours after that point.

Final note.

We'd like to thank everyone that has tried out papertrade over the last 10 days. It has been a labour of love building this product and both of us have been taken aback at all of the positive feedback we have received. We'd also like to thank all those of you who have spent considerable time musing on the system we have built, and much of your advice has been taken onboard and will likely affect the colour of what papertrade becomes going forward. We know some of these changes will be unpopular with some, but we would not be making them if we did not feel them to be absolutely necessary.

- blurr, jez

🧬 Virtual Embryo x Yukon 🧬

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.

text:
Five bangers from OpenAI's Karan Singhal:

1. Raising the floor and the ceiling of human health:

"There's more than 300 million people weekly using ChatGPT for health and wellness types of questions, and we take that as an incredibly important responsibility to get that right."

"We're really invested in making sure basically two things. One is that we can raise the floor of human health and give people access to trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence for free or nearly free, and really raise the ceiling as well and make things possible that weren't possible before."

2. Five physicians, eight answers:

"It turns out if you ask five physicians any question, you'll get, like, eight different answers. One of the first things that we did when we first started focusing on health at OpenAI was really build this kind of global physician network of hundreds of experts."

"[The goal was] to kind of aggregate the wisdom of experts so that we weren't relying, especially in areas where there could be disagreement, on one or two or three physicians to kind of adjudicate."

3. Why health runs on a general model rather than a specialized model:

"What we're talking about here is actually specialized training in a general model, which is, I think, actually the best of both worlds."

"If you forked and said, 'Hey, we're gonna train a smaller specialized model that is just for healthcare'... what you'd find is that model would fall behind the frontier relatively quickly, because the pace of the frontier and the general model improvements is so fast."

4. Compressing medicine's 5 to 17-year lag:

"How long does it take for clinical guidelines to penetrate the practice of everyday doctors across the world? People have found that this takes, depending on the study, 5 to 17 years... You don't wanna be practicing medicine 5 to 17 years behind."

"One of the things that we think about is how do you compress that kind of period of practicing down to weeks or days or even hours."

5. Healthcare's legacy software is ripe for agents:

"Healthcare is also one of those industries where you shouldn't expect everything to have an MCP connector tomorrow. It is a place where there's legacy software... This is absolutely ripe for agents and computer use."

 "This is a place where a lot of the barriers that have traditionally existed between patients and getting the care they need and clinicians and delivering the care they need and healthcare data in general... I think a lot of those will dissolve."

text:
My take on what happens now as a $PAPER staker (5 min read)

As shown in the first image, the PAPER emission curve will be very different after the next update.

The main question: How much long term yield can you  expect on PAPER staked today?

tl;dr ~$9k to ~$20k in yield per 1m PAPER in my opinion.

Two things to monitor:

1) The 'payout ratio' to stakers

Payout ratio is the net trader losses divided by the gross trader losses. I.e, for every $ lost on Papertrade, how much flows to stakers?

For this, see the second image. It has been at an average of 17.4% if you exclude the launch day where traders most likely tried to get liquidated more aggressively.

The payout ratio will have a big impact on how much yield you can expect on your staked PAPER over the long term and is mainly impacted by trader winnings relative to trader losses.

The final image shows the expected cumulative staking rewards per PAPER at different payout ratios. 

We can define the long term outcome as $2.5b in gross cumulative trader losses (10x what has been lost on Papertrade to date and above that you're so diluted you won't earn much additional yield).

If you expect the payout ratio to stay flat at 17.4%, long term you end up with 1.57 cents per PAPER which is $15.7k per 1m PAPER. 

I personally wouldn't be surprised to see the payout ratio trend down as I believe a significant share of recent trading has been attempts to realize negative PL in order to mint PAPER.

At 10%, the long term yield is $9k per 1m PAPER.

2) Will traders keep using Papertrade?

For the above-mentioned long term staking yield to be captured you need organic demand for the product. 

Traders have lost ~$250m so far since Papertrade went live 1.5 weeks ago. 

If this pace continues you'll realize the long term yield outcome in a few months but I'd expect the activity to slow down meaningfully after the week-1 hype. 

So potentially this 1-2c per PAPER in yield outcome could take a year or more depending on how much traction the protocol sees moving forward.

Keep in mind that this is an approximation, exact parameter upgrades haven't been specified yet.

I'd also argue that we very well could see the team tuning these parameters again in the future.

We could potentially see transferability at some point but I wouldn't count on it any time soon.

text:
I built a $1,000,000 paper quant desk.

Then I started breaking the market underneath it.

Watch 00:14.

Spreads jump 4×. Affected order books lose 87.5% of their available depth.

A SUI candidate still shows +11.75 bps after modelled costs.

Rejected.

The book has $68.8k of available depth. The desk requires $150k. A positive score doesn't get an exception.

That was the experiment: keep feeding the system attractive-looking candidates while making them harder to execute.

Across the full replay:

6,480 synthetic market snapshots.
6,029 rejected.
451 paper allocations.

Here's how the five roles divide the work:

1. SCOUT checks whether the snapshot is fresh and the spread is acceptable.
2. RESEARCH subtracts fees, spread, estimated slippage and a stress buffer from the proposed edge.
3. RED TEAM checks whether enough depth remains.
4. RISK caps each new allocation, total exposure and exposure to correlated assets.
5. EXECUTOR allocates paper capital only after the checks pass.

If you're building an AI trading agent, build this path before giving the model execution access:

Replay → costs → stress test → hard limits → paper execution → decision log.

Keep the proposed trade and its rejection reason together. Otherwise, debugging becomes reading a confident paragraph and guessing what went wrong.

This prototype uses synthetic data and five local, rule-based agent roles. No live LLM or broker is connected. The video is the actual terminal running.

Save the pipeline for your next agent build.

text:
Here is the prompt to build your own music MP3 player and internet radio for Amazon Alexa:

[ 🎶 Jukebox for Alexa ] by @levelsio 

Build me a private Alexa skill that plays my own music from a cloud bucket, plus internet radio

I want my Amazon Echo to play my own MP3s instead of being forced to use Amazon Music or Spotify. Build a private Alexa skill for this. Do as much as possible yourself: use CLIs and APIs, deploy and test it yourself, and only ask me for things only a person can do (logging in, clicking Allow, testing on the Echo).

Setup
- My music is in an S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2) under a music/ prefix. Each folder under it is a genre/playlist (music/Coffee Jazz/) or an artist/album (music/Artist/Album/).
- I'll create an access key for the bucket and give it to you. Keep it in a config file and never print it. The skill only needs read access; the upload tools need write access.
- My Echo and my Amazon developer account use the same Amazon login.

Build
1. An Alexa-hosted (Node.js) custom skill with invocation name "jukebox" (use two words if Amazon rejects one) and the AudioPlayer interface enabled.
2. Voice model: a PlayIntent with an AMAZON.SearchQuery slot ("play {query}", "put on {query}", "tune in to {query}", "shuffle {query}"), a ShuffleAllIntent, a WhatsPlayingIntent, a ListStationsIntent, and all the built-in AudioPlayer intents (pause, resume, next, previous, loop on/off, shuffle on/off, start over).
3. Library: list everything under music/ with ListObjectsV2 (follow the continuation token), build folders from the key prefixes, keep only .mp3/.m4a/.aac files, and cache the result for 5 minutes. Match spoken phrases to folder and file names loosely: ignore track numbers and spacing ("ama piano" = amapiano), turn number words into digits ("thirteen beaches" = 13 Beaches), and handle genre aliases (dnb, drum n bass, hiphop, lo fi).
4. Playback: give Alexa a presigned HTTPS GET URL for each file. Make it valid for at least 12 hours so long mixes and pause/resume don't expire mid-play. Keep the bucket private. Store the play queue in the AudioPlayer token (folder, shuffle seed, position) so there's no database, and enqueue the next track on PlaybackNearlyFinished. Folders shuffle and loop. A folder whose files all start with track numbers is an album and plays in order. A single song carries on with the rest of its folder.
5. Radio: a stations list of HTTPS MP3/AAC/HLS streams, with good underground electronic stations (Rinse FM, NTS, Bassdrive, Intergalactic FM, Kiosk Radio, Refuge Worldwide, and so on) plus news (BBC World Service, NPR). Test every URL with curl first and drop the plain-HTTP ones, because Alexa refuses them. Support "play rinse fm", "drum and bass radio", "techno radio" and "the news", and make next/previous switch stations. Live streams drop and Alexa treats a drop as the end, so re-enqueue the same stream with a new token on PlaybackNearlyFinished, and retry once on PlaybackFailed.
6. Log one line per request (type, intent, token, offset, error) so playback problems show up in CloudWatch.

Deploy without the web console
- Install the ASK CLI (npm i -g ask-cli). If ask configure won't work in your shell, run ask util generate-lwa-tokens --no-browser, have me paste the one-time code, and write ~/.ask/cli_config yourself. Get the vendor ID from GET https://t.co/8eS787CaBt.
- The hosted skill's code is a git repo (find it with ask smapi get-alexa-hosted-skill-metadata). Push to master to deploy, with ask util git-credentials-helper as the git credential helper. The helper needs ask-resources.json and .ask/ask-states.json next to the repo. If pushes start failing with 403, clear the cached macOS keychain credential.
- The hosted runtime may run an old Node version, so pin an S3 SDK version that supports it, or sign URLs with a small SigV4 library.
- Upload the voice model with ask smapi set-interaction-model, check the skill manifest lists AUDIO_PLAYER, and test with ask smapi simulate-skill. The web console's simulator can't play audio, so a "problem with the requested skill's response" error there is expected.

When it works, tell me how to add Alexa app routines (When: voice "coffee jazz" → Action: Customized "ask jukebox to play coffee jazz") so I can just say "Alexa, coffee jazz". And how to play internet radio stations I like.

text:
I believe the most valuable aspect of researching $Pokémon is no longer just the hype surrounding Pokémon culture and Pumpfun's new features.

D42TjMjz5H7toPu5md5KBXreZkCSdZMEfLQwmBhJXvb1

It's whether it has the potential to become the common quote asset within this ecosystem.

Pumpfun recently launched a card pack opening feature, connecting trading card games such as Pokémon with the platform's trading experience. Meanwhile, Collector Crypt ($CARDS) connects physical graded cards with on-chain assets, giving Pokémon-themed tokens a new narrative. For the market, this is not simply another IP to speculate on. Collecting, pack openings, asset trading, and Meme token launches are beginning to come together within the same ecosystem.

I believe Pokémon's advantage here goes beyond brand recognition. Pack openings inherently involve randomness, rarity, and the desire to collect. Players chase rare cards and compare their collections. This culture is naturally suited to gamification, showcasing, and sharing. By bringing pack openings into its existing app, Pumpfun gives users the opportunity to access cards, trade tokens, and speculate on or create content around different Pokémon-themed projects within the same platform.

However, these factors only explain why Pokémon-themed tokens have attracted new attention. They are not enough to explain why Pokémon deserves particular attention. What really interests me is the role it is attempting to play within this ecosystem.

According to Global Trade Station's design, Pokémon is not just an independently traded Meme. It is paired with CARDS, while other Pumpfun projects can also choose Pokémon as their trading pair. Projects that meet the relevant requirements and complete migration can enter the ecosystem's numbered registration system, with rarity tiers assigned according to market capitalization.

This design makes me think that Pokémon's original collecting logic is being brought into the token issuance system. Each new project can have its own theme, number, and rarity, while Pokémon attempts to become the common asset connecting these projects.

If more creators choose to launch tokens using Pokémon as their trading pair in the future, the market will no longer be trading just one Pokémon-themed coin. Instead, it could be trading a collection of new pairs built around the same quote asset. Each project can have its own independent narrative while sharing a common entry point into the ecosystem.

This is what makes Pokémon more interesting to me than an ordinary themed Meme: it is attempting to evolve from a token that attracts attention through cultural hype into one of the trading infrastructure assets of an entire ecosystem.

Of course, the existence of trading pairs does not guarantee that Pokémon will rise. When other tokens use it as their trading pair, their trading activity becomes connected to Pokémon, but transactions work in both directions. An increase in the number of projects and liquidity pools does not necessarily mean that real demand is increasing. If these projects cannot generate sustained trading volume and sufficient liquidity, even a seemingly large ecosystem may fail to create meaningful economic value for Pokémon.

The holder reward data from the past ten hours provides another angle worth observing.

The Pokémon page shows that the entire 0.3% Creator Fee generated by each transaction is distributed to holders, with rewards paid in CARDS. In the two screenshots you provided, cumulative distributions increased from 31.5K CARDS to 46.8K, an increase of approximately 48.6%. The cumulative number of distribution payments increased from around 9,930 to 31,500, a rise of approximately 217%.

What interests me more is that the number of distribution payments grew significantly faster than the total amount distributed. This indicates that distribution events have become more frequent, but the average amount of CARDS per distribution has actually decreased by roughly half. Therefore, these figures demonstrate that the distribution mechanism is operating continuously, but they do not directly imply that every holder's rewards are increasing.

There is another distinction that is easy to overlook: holders receive CARDS, not Pokémon itself. Rewards can give participants an additional incentive to hold the token, but their actual appeal also depends on the price, liquidity, and supply changes of CARDS. This is not a buyback-and-burn mechanism for Pokémon, nor can it be directly equated with stable token revenue.

Therefore, I would not treat this reward design as the main bullish thesis. What matters more to me is whether it can reinforce the paired-token ecosystem. If more new tokens adopt Pokémon as their trading pair, the liquidity pools generate sustained trading activity, and the reward mechanism continues operating, holders will have more reasons to pay attention to the development of the entire ecosystem rather than simply waiting for the price of Pokémon itself to rise.

The most interesting aspect of this mechanism is the potential for a network effect: more projects adopt Pokémon, expanding the reach of the paired-token ecosystem; more trading activity creates a more direct connection between the quote asset and the broader ecosystem; meanwhile, trading card collecting and pack opening features continue to bring new content and participants into the Pokémon-themed market.

However, this logic depends on one prerequisite: the paired-token ecosystem must generate genuine, sustained trading demand rather than simply creating a large number of low-liquidity tokens.

I will also continue monitoring CARDS because it serves both as the paired asset for Pokémon and as the asset used to pay holder rewards. If the price or liquidity of CARDS is affected by supply unlocks, the actual value of rewards and the trading structure of the paired tokens could also change. Previously published tokenomics information indicated that, after October 29, 2026, CARDS would have monthly unlocks of approximately 44.6 million tokens, equivalent to around 2.2% of its total supply. Whether these tokens create selling pressure will still depend on the actual unlocks and holder behavior, but this is a variable that cannot be ignored when assessing the sustainability of the reward mechanism.

Another boundary is intellectual property. Pokémon is a globally recognized cultural brand, but there is currently no evidence that this Pokémon token has official authorization from Pokémon. Its cultural recognition can help it attract attention, but that does not translate directly into official endorsement or a guaranteed asset value.

Therefore, what I most want to verify now is not whether Pokémon can rise again because of Pokémon hype, but whether it can truly become a common quote asset that other projects are willing to use. Going forward, I will focus on whether the number of tokens using it as a trading pair continues to increase, whether these liquidity pools can generate stable trading volume, and whether ecosystem activity can create sustained real demand.

If these three aspects are gradually validated, the growth thesis for Pokémon could go beyond a purely cultural narrative. Its value would no longer depend solely on how popular Pokémon is, but on how many projects are willing to establish trading relationships around it and whether those relationships can continually generate actual economic activity.

For me, this is the direction Pokémon is most worth betting on: not becoming yet another Meme that rises on Pokémon hype, but potentially becoming a common asset connecting Pokémon-themed tokens, collectible card assets, and the Pumpfun trading ecosystem.

Ultimately, what determines how far it can go will not be how many new tokens appear in the ecosystem, but whether those tokens actually need it.

Every position has a risk number behind it: a credit line, a derivatives book, a portfolio, a treasury. That number mostly comes from a model or a committee, and its track record is rarely public.

Endure turns it into a competition: forecasters put risk estimates on the line, a network scores them against reality, and the best forecasters earn the weight. Today that runs on 15 subnets, every day, and it’s where we start.

The loop is built for exposures that can be written down as numbers and checked later.

🧬 Virtual Embryo x Yukon 🧬

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.
