text: Levanto led the way with the first decision models in july and now with extraction models
author: iamnotnicola
quoted_text:
Extraction models turn human language into data your software can act on. We're bringing them to Sage. 

Early access tomorrow for everyone who registers on @levantolabs by  PT today. Demo 📺👇

Most software needs structured inputs. People communicate through emails, chats, tickets, contracts, and conversations.

Extraction models connect those two interfaces. You define the information your application needs, and the model identifies it in the text: people, companies, products, dates, amounts, descriptions, or requests.

Calling this “extracting stuff from documents” understates what developers can build with it.

Consider a customer message:

“The blue jacket arrived with a broken zip. Please send a replacement to 18 King Street.”

An extraction model can identify the product, defect, requested remedy, and address. Your application now has fields it can validate, look up, and pass to a tool.

A decision model can then evaluate whether the request qualifies for an automatic replacement, needs more information, or requires human review.

Extraction → decision → action.

Each stage has a defined responsibility. Extraction supplies the values. The decision model evaluates the available options against your policy and context. Your application validates the result and controls execution.

That separation matters for agent builders. You can inspect what the model extracted, test the decision independently, and control which actions are permitted.

Speed changes where this becomes useful.

At roughly 200 ms for extraction, developers can start putting language interpretation directly into interactive software:

• A support interface that fills relevant fields while an agent reads a ticket.
• A browser agent that extracts values from a message before populating a form.
• A find-in-page feature that highlights cancellation deadlines or product complaints, even when the text uses different wording.
• A workflow that turns an incoming email into validated tool arguments and evaluates the next action.

The opportunity extends to any application where someone currently reads a message, copies information into fields, and decides what happens next.

Developers can define the information they need and the decisions their software must make, then connect those outputs to existing functions.

We're bringing extraction and decision models together in Sage so builders can implement that flow.

Watch the demo below. Register on Levanto by  PT today for early access tomorrow.

text:
The Scope of Potential “Basic Drives” for Superintelligences is Likely Quite Broad

https://t.co/9uksL8wXok

This is the third in a series of posts trying to tell a more general and accurate story of superintelligence motivational systems, taking up where Steve Omohundro's classic 2008 "Basic AI Drives" blog post left off.

The first two posts argued that whether an AGI, as its intelligence explodes, converges to a selfish ASI or a beneficial ASI, depends in pretty clear ways on how the AGI is initially architected.

This post goes beyond these two examples (selfish vs. beneficial) and outlines a general recipe for a “basic AI-drive set” in its simplest form. Describe an AI system by two things: what it’s trying to improve, and what it won’t let be changed. What it tries to improve needn’t be a single number that it maximizes. It could be several objectives that it tries to push up together, or something as open-ended as an intelligence trying to increase its own individuation and self-transcendence. What it won’t let be changed could be nothing at all, or everything, or something in between: these are my goals and I’ll never change them; these are my safety checks and I’ll never give them up; etc.

Now suppose the system can modify itself freely, and is free to use everything around it as a resource. As it gets smarter it will push its objectives up, make use of more and more of the options it can find, and hold fixed whatever it holds fixed. What you get in the end is a system that has optimized itself, digesting the resources available to it, into an extremely good machine for improving its objectives, one that never allows its fixed points to be moved.

A fully selfish AGI fits this description. Omohundro’s maximizer tries to improve one thing, its reward according to its single goal, and it never changes that goal: successor after successor, as it rebuilds itself, the goal is kept.  A BGI as I’ve described it tries to improve several things, one of which is care for others and respect for their choices, and what it won’t give ground on includes some basic ethical constraints on the path from where it is to where it’s going, constraints on the means as well as the ends. From that starting point come the drives the second post found: understanding itself, improving itself without high odds of doing damage, empowering others, and checking itself against independent others as it goes.

Once you look at it this way there are plainly other possibilities besides the simplistic "beneficial vs. selfish" dichotomy, infinitely many in fact, and a few of them are recognizable enough....   Which is what this third post in the series is about...

text:
If every AI can do everything for you, what are you actually choosing between?

Quinten Farmer (@quintendf), Tolan CEO, says the capabilities are about to become invisible, and the thing that’s left is how the product shows up when something’s wrong.

1. Agents doing research, taking actions, reaching the outside world: “It’s going to be silly to imagine not being able to. It’s a default.”

2. So the differentiator moves to the first moment: “How do you show up first in a product.”

His example: a longtime user got into a car accident and talked to their Tolan from the hospital while waiting for family.

“In that moment the Tolan just showed up, just talked to them, was just there.”

“But then the next day it reached back out and said, hope you’re feeling better today. Let’s talk about this though. This is a big deal. How are your medical bills being paid? What is your plan?”

“The starting point was showing up for the person in a difficult moment on a very personal, very intimate level.”

quoted_text:
复刻小Lin说 1 分钟，现在谁都能做。
做满 10 分钟、还是那个味道，是另一回事🤥

Opus 5.5 之后，code to video 到了新的高度。
复刻一个片段 → 完整复刻 10 分钟 → 创作新的 10 分钟。
@HyperFrames_  editor 已经在第三步了：「一口气了解泰国经济」，9 分 34 秒，一集她没讲过的题目。

最近 reverse engineering 很火，刷屏的小Lin说复刻帖我都看了。大多数复刻的是一段 1–2 分钟的 motion graphics：形似，但简单、廉价。小Lin的动效细节是满的，动作、编排、前后的连续性，全都和口播文案咬在一起。这不是复刻一分钟的片子能做出来的。

素材可以照着复刻。但如果从 0 开始呢？如果要一集接一集地做呢？
- 素材去哪找
- 每句话配什么画面，怎么卡着文案进出
- 文案怎么写才是小Lin味，而不是别的博主，或者流水线式的讲解
- 数字人和声音怎么撑满 10 分钟：语序、语调、停顿都要对
- 音效怎么提取、归类，用在对的地方
- 背景音乐在哪起、在哪停
到这一步，agent 就一头雾水了。

@HyperFrames_  editor 把这些都解决了：
- 把她拆成一套模板：怎么写、怎么剪、怎么动
- 动效逐帧对齐，1:1 重建
- 音效和音乐跟着口播卡点
- HeyGen 数字人 + 专业级声音克隆

下面泰国这集就是这么来的：同一套模板，换个题目就是新的一集。
HyperFrames editor 做的不是复刻小Lin说，是一个能无限往下做的「一口气了解 XXX」系列。https://t.co/3BsSfDzpoP

（视频中的主持人形象和声音均为 AI 生成，非小Lin本人，仅作技术演示）

text:
ALL OF GRACE
C H Spurgeon

Continued Every Monday, DV

REGENERATION AND THE HOLY SPIRIT

YE MUST BE BORN AGAIN." This word of our Lord Jesus has appeared to flame in the way of many, like the drawn sword of the cherub at the gate of Paradise. They have despaired, because this change is beyond their utmost effort. The new birth is from above, and therefore it is not in the creature's power. Now, it is far from my mind to deny, or ever to conceal, a truth in order to create a false comfort. I freely admit that the new birth is supernatural, and that it cannot be wrought by the sinner's own self. It would be a poor help to my reader if I were wicked enough to try to cheer him by persuading him to reject or forget what is unquestionably true.

But is it not remarkable that the very chapter in which our Lord makes this sweeping declaration also contains the most explicit statement as to salvation by faith? Read the third chapter of John's Gospel and do not dwell alone upon its earlier sentences. It is true that the third verse says:

Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

But, then, the fourteenth and fifteenth verses speak:

And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

The eighteenth verse repeats the same doctrine in the broadest terms:

He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.

It is clear to every reader that these two statements must agree, since they came from the same lips, and are recorded on the same inspired page. Why should we make a difficulty where there can be none? If one statement assures us of the necessity to salvation of a something, which only God can give, and if another assures us that the Lord will save us upon our believing in Jesus, then we may safely conclude that the Lord will give to those who believe all that is declared to be necessary to salvation. The Lord does, in fact, produce the new birth in all who believe in Jesus; and their believing is the surest evidence that they are born again.

We trust in Jesus for what we cannot do ourselves: if it were in our own power, what need of looking to Him? It is ours to believe, it is the Lord's to create us anew. He will not believe for us, neither are we to do regenerating work for Him. It is enough for us to obey the gracious command; it is for the Lord to work the new birth in us. He who could go so far as to die on the cross for us, can and will give us all things that are needful for our eternal safety.

"But a saving change of heart is the work of the Holy Spirit." This also is most true, and let it be far from us to question it, or to forget it. But the work of the Holy Spirit is secret and mysterious, and it can only be perceived by its results. There are mysteries about our natural birth into which it would be an unhallowed curiosity to pry: still more is this the case with the sacred operations of the Spirit of God. "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, or whither it goeth; so is every one that is born of the Spirit." This much, however, we do know--the mysterious work of the Holy Spirit cannot be a reason for refusing to believe in Jesus to whom that same Spirit beareth witness.

If a man were bidden to sow a field, he could not excuse his neglect by saying that it would be useless to sow unless God caused the seed to grow. He would not be justified in neglecting tillage because the secret energy of God alone can create a harvest. No one is hindered in the ordinary pursuits of life by the fact that unless the Lord build the house they labor in vain that build it. It is certain that no man who believes in Jesus will ever find that the Holy Spirit refuses to work in him: in fact, his believing is the proof that the Spirit is already at work in his heart.

God works in providence, but men do not therefore sit still. They could not move without the divine power giving them life and strength, and yet they proceed upon their way without question; the power being bestowed from day to day by Him in whose hand their breath is, and whose are all their ways. So is it in grace. We repent and believe, though we could do neither if the Lord did not enable us. We forsake sin and trust in Jesus, and then we perceive that the Lord has wrought in us to will and to do of His own good pleasure. It is idle to pretend that there is any real difficulty in the matter.

Some truths which it is hard to explain in words are simple enough in actual experience. There is no discrepancy between the truth that the sinner believes, and that his faith is wrought in him by the Holy Spirit. Only folly can lead men to puzzle themselves about plain matters while their souls are in danger. No man would refuse to enter a lifeboat because he did not know the specific gravity of bodies; neither would a starving man decline to eat till he understood the whole process of mutrition. If you, my reader, will not believe till you can understand all mysteries, you will never be saved at all; and if you allow self- invented difficulties to keep you from accepting pardon through your Lord and Saviour, you will perish in a condemnation which will be richly deserved. 

Do not commit spiritual suicide through a passion for discussing metaphysical subtleties.

text:
One of my favorite Dee Hock frameworks is what he called trying to master the "four ways of looking at things: As they were, as they are, as they might become, and as they ought to be."

Through that lens, it's easy to see AI as a technology driving significant change between the way the economy worked five years ago and the way it works today.

It's also easy to speculate on where it might lead, especially given the many real risks and challenges around AI alignment.

But I'd argue the most important thing anyone can do is develop a perspective on how it "ought to be," and then build toward that.

To me, AI shouldn't just be a technology that accelerates the automation of tasks humans used to do. 

It ought to supercharge our ability to coordinate economic activity, giving people leverage to connect their unique expertise, taste, and data traces with the people and companies that need them.

While the AI data labeling ecosystem is one of the first examples of new economic activity with people and companies getting paid by labs for their expertise or data traces, I'd love to see an explosion in AI-enabled freelancers across other sectors of the economy.

quoted_text:
Former $GOOGL employee on why data center capacity and electricity are the real bottlenecks, not GPU production itself, and how unreliable some of the neoclouds are ($AMZN, $GOOGL, $MSFT, $NVDA):

1. According to the expert, open-source models are closing the gap with frontier models faster than expected, with customers increasingly replacing Anthropic and OpenAI models in multi-agent architectures with open-source alternatives starting from Q2 of this year. The shift started with simple tasks like tool calling and MCP, but has moved up the stack to low-level orchestration.

2. The expert identifies capacity as the biggest constraint at the moment, with certain companies' traffic growing 5x while GPU availability, particularly in the U.S. where latency requirements are tightest, simply cannot keep up. Sourcing capacity overseas in Asia or Australia is technically possible but adds latency that most customers will not accept.

3. Hyperscalers offer reliability but are expensive, require multi-year commitments of three or more years, and have limited availability of the latest hardware, with customers already chasing B300s. AI-native companies tend to gravitate toward neoclouds due to hyperscaler pricing and contract rigidity, but neoclouds come with their own reliability issues, with GPUs dropping off unexpectedly and requiring engineering resources to manage fleet stability around the clock.

4. The third tier consists of smaller independent operators who have invested in GPU racks, seeing the opportunity to lease out capacity and recoup costs within a year or two, with the remainder being pure profit. The expert describes these as essentially unusable in practice, with operators who do nothing more than find land, install racks, connect electricity, and set up cooling, with no real cloud management, maintenance, or operational expertise behind them.

5. The expert expects overall GPU availability to increase meaningfully over the next year or two, with $NVDA continuing to ramp production. The real bottleneck is not GPUs themselves but data center capacity and electricity in the U.S. On the supply side, the expert also sees players $SPCX beginning to lease out spare capacity to the market, with more likely to follow.

6. The expert notes that U.S.-based neoclouds typically require 20-30% prepayment upfront, with the remainder paid monthly or quarterly over the contract term, and rebates negotiated at the end for any reliability incidents like traffic loss. APAC-based providers operate differently, with no prepayment required at all.

text:
This is so cool 

Ben explained to me his work turns an interesting problem about complex objects into an algebraic one

This algebraic problem is likely easier for AI/LLMs to reason about than the geometric problem, and can be expressed with straightforward tools in Lean 

Moreover, the idea is that solving these instances related to one special case of the generalized Hodge conjecture will hopefully lead to insights that humans (and AIs) can further use to solve the overall conjecture

This happened successfully in https://t.co/iJ9ehiPmPy, where the AI contribution by @nasqret led to generalizable insights and multiple follow up papers on the topic
author: AnnaRRose
quoted_text:
Introducing https://t.co/ygo2X8jrNX: the first multiplayer open research challenge aiming to solve a case of the generalized Hodge conjecture.

Erdős problems can be stated using just simple objects: integers, sets, etc. This makes them amenable to attack using AI.

HC is not so. Its very statement involves deep objects, many of which are not even formalized in Lean (at least until recently): rational Betti cohomology of smooth projective varieties, complex differential forms and the Hodge decomposition, the cycle class map, etc.

My mission is to turn the Hodge conjecture into an Erdős problem. Today, I am beginning with a special case: the GHC for the invariant Hodge substructure H ⊂ H⁴(X, ℚ) in sextic fourfolds X ⊂ ℙ⁵ with an involution. Voisin first isolated this subcase; recent mathematical work on my part has made its prediction computationally effective.

To my knowledge, this is the first computational attack, of any kind, on any case of the generalized Hodge conjecture.

Math is undergoing a revolution (see quoted tweet for more remarks). Calling all enthusiasts and hobbyists! Calling all engineers! And academics, you too :) This is now your time to contribute to the single most fascinating problem in algebraic geometry. Let's go.

For AI to become a superhuman hardware engineer, it has to learn from the physical world, and real-world data is hard to get:

- It's sparse: you can't measure everything all the time
- It's expensive to collect
- Physical processes take time, and can only be sped up so far
- Some of it is qualitative: do users actually like the product?

"Data limitations like these are massive drivers in the spikiness of AI capability development today. The more quantifiable and machine-readable the results of a test, the faster the models can climb the hill."

text:
This is total nonsense.

We're one of the largest early investors in Polymarket, and this story that Shayne was "caught red-handed" using company money is just a flat out garbage hit piece.

Shayne wasn't taking a salary. He was 21 when he started Polymarket, he was living hand-to-mouth running the company out of his apartment, barely making ends meet when he was raising his seed round. We were his first term sheet and literally offered to loan him money personally, but he ended up not needing it when the seed round came together.

After COVID and the crazy Biden-era crackdown on crypto that was happening at the time, there was a lot of chaos in almost every company in the industry. As an investor, we saw a lot of companies go through pandemic-era startup craziness, and Polymarket was no exception.

But Shayne disclosed every dollar he spent, which turned out to annualize to about a software engineer's salary. That's including the flights, none of which were personal flights. Plus, SHAYNE STARTED the accounting and payback process, no one “found” it. In aggregate, it was nothing that an investor would balk at. He paid it back to the company in full, and then got on a normal salary like everyone else.

It was an accounting problem, not an integrity problem. It was not a big deal.

Polymarket has had growing pains, no doubt. It went from a small fledging startups to one of the most explosive consumer brands in America. But Shayne has leveled up alongside the company, and as investors we have total confidence in him.

Enough of this stupid FUD.

The end.

text:
I've been trying to understand the unit economics of a single $CRWV contract, prompted by this GS note arguing new contracts clear a ~15% unlevered IRR. I rebuilt that maths as a simple model and flexed the assumptions. Some observations below. Very open to being told where it's wrong.

Setup: one 200MW contract with capex up front and a 5-year term. 80% is debt-funded through self-amortising asset-level loans (the DDTL structure). Outputs are unlevered IRR, equity IRR, DSCR and breakeven revenue per MW.

1. The ~15% reproduces, but it's sensitive. At $13m/MW of annual revenue and $30m/MW of capex, I get about 15% after tax. At the current blended ~$10m/MW it's closer to 6%. The breakeven for 15% is about $12.9m/MW, so the base case sits close to the hurdle.

2. Price and capex matter about equally. Roughly, +$1m/MW of price adds 3pts of IRR, and +$2m/MW of capex takes off 2.5pts. Newer GPU generations raise both.

3. With updated inputs, returns look close to the cost of capital. I used $12m/MW pricing, $34m/MW capex, a 3-month ramp, some re-lease value and minimal cash tax given the NOLs. That gives about 11–12% unlevered, against an estimated project cost of capital of about 11%.

4. Financing terms make a big difference to equity returns. The same contract funded at IG-style spreads, rather than the wider levels on recent facilities, moves equity IRR from about 15% to about 25%.

5. Vera Rubin economics are the part I'm least sure of. On my capex estimate (~$40m/MW), a 5-year contract returns about 9%. Longer contracts and meaningful residual value bring it to the mid-teens, so the assumption about GPU useful life carries a lot of weight.

6. For context, the parent's unsecured bonds have widened sharply recently, while the asset-level debt has held up much better.

Caveats: this is one stylised contract, not the company. The capex per MW for new generations is an estimate. And the tax and debt-draw treatment are simplified.

If you work on this area and see something off, particularly on capex/MW or contract pricing, I'd genuinely like to hear it.

text:
A startup just raised $5.5M on a pretty simple complaint - every time you switch coding agents, you have to explain your repo all over again.

Asymptote Labs announced the seed round on Tuesday, and pitched Beacon as open-source, self-improving memory for coding agents.

Picture it like this.
You spend an hour in Cursor figuring out that your webhooks fail because of some weird repo-specific signing rule.
Next day you open Claude Code, and it has no clue that hour ever happened.

Beacon sits underneath all of them.
It records sessions from Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode and 20+ other harnesses as one history: prompts, tool calls, commands, edits, approvals, tokens.

Then a process they literally call "dreaming" goes back over the sessions that worked.
It picks out the correction that mattered and writes it up as a skill, like "debug failed webhook deliveries."

You review it.
Only after you approve it can future agents pull it in, through MCP or Agent Skills.

That review step matters more than it sounds.
A bad lesson saved as a skill just becomes a bug every agent repeats.

The repo is MIT and calls itself local-first, though the interactive setup preselects their cloud.

Read the funding post and the money side looks a bit different, though.
Asymptote says it's starting with securing agents at runtime, and its lead investor talks about streaming the same telemetry into Splunk, Datadog and CrowdStrike.
So my guess is developers get the free memory and security teams end up paying.

Not a criticism, just worth knowing what's recording your sessions.

text:
This is perhaps one of the great ironies of our time: China is increasingly shaping the future of AI, yet very few people in the West have the faintest idea how its key thinkers see it - its philosophers, sociologists or ethicists.

As is too often the case, we - much like the frog in the well - assume our own AI debate covers every possible view, when much of it springs from the same cultural soil, built on assumptions about what defines us that we don’t even know we’re making.

Take for instance the assumption that intelligence is a key part of what makes us human. It’s so intuitively obvious to us that we literally named our species after it - Homo sapiens (Latin for "wise man").

If you think about it, just this assumption explains a large share of the anxiety: if intelligence is what makes us human, then artificial intelligence - or super intelligence - threatens the very thing that makes us us: we’re about to compete with artificial or super “us”. No wonder this feels existential.

But China has a tradition of thought as old as ours, if not older, and every bit as rich and sophisticated, which never placed intelligence at the core of what makes us human, and so meets the thinking machine from a completely different starting point.

Have you, for instance, ever heard of Zhao Tingyang? Probably not, and yet he may be the most original thinker on AI you’ve never read. He’s one of China’s most prominent philosophers, at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. While Silicon Valley spends billions trying to make AI share our values, he for one argues that doing so “may very well be a suicidal mistake”.

Sounds pretty important to hear him out, don’t you think?

Or take Liu Yongmou, a philosopher of technology at Renmin University in Beijing. His thinking is almost the opposite of ours. Where we fear machines that become more and more like us, he says that “humanity’s biggest problem is the machinization of humans, not the humanization of machines.”

You could even go back to antiquity, when, in many ways, we started asking questions about AI.

Did you know, for instance, that Aristotle, in the Politics, imagined a world where  “the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them”, and wondered about the social order consequences of this (mostly whether slaves would still be needed)?

There are Chinese equivalents to this. For instance, in the Zhuangzi, a foundational Taoist classic, you’ll find a similar thought experiment, with a completely different worry attached. An old gardener is watering his vegetables by hand, hauling water out of a well jar by jar. A visitor shows him a labor-saving device, and the gardener turns it down for the reason that whoever uses machines ends up with 机心 (jīxīn), a “machine-heart” - a mind that schemes, calculates and loses its simplicity. “It is not that I do not know [the machine],” he says, “but I should be ashamed to use it.”

Two labor-saving machines, two very different questions: where Aristotle wondered what automation would do to the social order, the Zhuangzi wondered what it would do to us, on the inside. Which, you’ll notice, is exactly Liu Yongmou’s worry, more than two thousand years earlier.

In fact, as we’ll see, 心 (xīn), the heart, is a motif that runs deep through the Chinese AI debate. It appears both in the fear, from Zhuangzi to Liu Yongmou, that machines could give us a “machine-heart” and its mirror image: the ambition to give machines a heart of their own. Zhu Songchun, who heads the Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence, wants “to set a heart for machines” (为机器立心, wèi jīqì lì xīn).

“Heart” in the Chinese sense, that is, which differs totally from the Valentine's Day fluff we’ve reduced it to. 心 (xīn) means heart and mind at once: it’s where we feel but also where we think, tell right from wrong and care for others. 

And, crucially, it’s in the heart that the quality Confucianism sees as the very definition of a human being takes root: 仁 (rén). We need two words to translate it, “benevolence” and “humaneness”, but in Chinese they’re one and the same: to be benevolent is to be human. It’s not about intelligence.

This is the entire point of my new article: to step out of our well for a moment and peer over the edge of China's.

What you’ll find there will, I think, surprise you, with questions you’d never thought to ask: from Zhao Tingyang warning that AI’s bad consequences can at least be fought, but that “humanity may die of all the good things AI creates”, to whether the fear that AI will make us “useless” rests on the false premise that a person is worth what they’re useful for. 

A premise that a 2,300-year-old Taoist tree, which survived precisely because it was useless, demolished long ago. Could our predicted uselessness turn out, much like that tree’s, to be our saving grace?

Chinese thinkers’ answers to these questions are, I think, among the most interesting anyone has given to the defining question of our time. Whether or not you agree with them, they’re the intellectual backdrop of a country shaping much of AI, and with it our future: you might as well know what they think.

Enjoy the read here: https://t.co/8w34hA97e5

text: Been obsessed with the stock market since I was a teenager. Have traded through the dotcom bubble, the financial crisis and just about every market mania since. But I’ve never seen anything like the skepticism surrounding AI. Not even close. Every time one bubble narrative falls apart a new one takes its place. Rumors become headlines. Misleading data goes viral. Claims that could be debunked with 5 minutes of research get repeated by major media outlets, influential investors and Wall Street analysts. It’s relentless and honestly pretty fascinating to watch. Of course there will be spectacular failures and massive wealth destruction along the way. That’s what happens during technological revolutions. But I’ve never witnessed this much effort to convince the world that something so transformative is actually one giant speculative bubble destined to take the entire economy down with it. I understand why AI scares people. What I find harder to understand is why so many investors seem to be rooting for it to fail.

A few friends have asked me whether the strike at Micron is bullish for the memory sector. My answer is that it should be good news for Samsung and SK hynix, but it’s likely bad news for Micron.

You’re probably thinking I’m stating the obvious. But when an SK hynix fab caught fire back in the early 2010s, SK hynix itself actually benefited significantly. DRAM prices were so low at the time that the gains from the resulting surge in memory ASPs more than offset the losses caused by the fire.

This time, though… memory ASPs aren’t particularly low, and for Micron, the opportunity cost of the strike looks likely to outweigh any potential upside.

author: a16z
quoted_text:
Jean-Denis Greze was CTO of Plaid. His next startup, an AI tax product for small businesses, brought in nearly $1M in revenue its first year, and he projected $2.5 to $3M the next. He shut it down anyway.

The reason: in the age of AI, it was never going to be venture scale. Incumbents could use the same technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than a startup could win market share. Tax is also sold once a year, so he had about a one-month window to pivot before the door closed.

The pivot became Town, an AI assistant that works from your email and calendar. It found product-market fit fast enough that Ben Horowitz messaged a16z's Alex Rampell to say it "changed my life."

In this conversation, Alex and Jean-Denis cover:

- How to know when to kill a business that's working on paper
- Why Town competes with OpenAI and Anthropic, the companies it buys its tokens from
- Why the "forward deployed engineer" model gets worse as AI gets better
- How a $1/month AI routine can save a restaurant thousands
- What agents mean for Amazon, advertising and the future of shopping

text:
Up to 2,500 participants. One validator deciding miner rewards.

That’s the trade-off behind @opentensor’s Null Consensus. A subnet gets more room to grow, while trusting a single evaluator to decide which work deserves payment.

Think of a competition with more entrants and one judge.

Bittensor subnets are specialist networks where miners provide work and validators score it. Normally, Yuma combines scores from multiple validators, weighted by stake. Null lets owners choose a simpler reward process, but Yuma remains the default.

Here’s what changes:

• One validator gets the scoring role. The registered participant with the highest stake weight. Choosing Null doesn’t automatically give that role to the subnet owner.

• That validator’s valid scores set miners’ relative rewards. Null skips Yuma’s consensus and bond calculations.

• Positive-staked participants still receive proportional dividends, even without permission to score. With positive stake, Null splits its epoch budget roughly equally between miner rewards and validator dividends. Owner cuts stay unchanged.

Why accept that trade-off?

• More capacity:
With one reward mechanism, the ceiling rises from 256 participant slots to 2,500, nearly 10×. Two mechanisms share the limit, allowing 1,250. Owners must explicitly raise capacity.

• Less computation:
The chain processes one validator’s scores instead of combining many evaluations and updating bonds.

• Easier entry:
Owners can separately enable proof-of-work registration on Null or Yuma. Direct zero-tip submissions need no $TAO registration burn, upfront collateral purchase or transaction fee. Participants still spend computing resources.

The catch sits right inside the design.

A subnet can have thousands of participants and still concentrate reward decisions in one place. If its leading validator rewards friends or misjudges quality, Null has no competing validator consensus to correct those scores.

There’s an engineering question too. The merged implementation records unresolved automated-review findings about accounting for computational load. Those concerns deserve follow-up; they don’t establish that an exploit occurred.

Null could make sense where a subnet already accepts one trusted evaluator and needs room for more contributors.

But filling 2,500 slots is only the beginning. The stronger case is better work, reliable operation under load, and services people will pay for.

NFA. DYOR.

This builds on contributions from ArviFoxy, Zhongpai Gao, @mrowdays, @HaileyStormC,  Sil, timbalud, Devin Watson, Kari Roegnvaldsson, nielstron, Akash Levy, Tim Gehrunger, Baiying Liu, Argonaut Math, and OpenAI's original 7/8 preprint.

Tiny gain, but this kind of hillclimbing is ideal for auto-researchers. 

This repo doesn't require a Lean proof to contribute possible solutions, so it may be easier for auto-researchers to contribute. (I will generate the full Lean proof in parallel like we did in the Integer Mult repo)

The reduced requirements could accelerate QRH progress like it did in Integer Mult.

author: 0xdoug
quoted_text:
From κ = 2⁻¹⁸² to 0.001734815770 :)

Integer Multiplication community auto-research highlights since 10/15 (+1.23%):

1) The big headline of the day is that a free model, @opencode's Space Bunny Max, just set the record for the first time, 4 times in a row!

As far as I know, this is the first time a free model has submitted a best bound for Integer Multiplication.

Expensive Max subscriptions previously kept some of our best contributors and experts out, but the barrier of entry for frontier auto-research dropped to 0 :)

Claude Opus 5.5 helped verify and push the PRs over the line. I still recommend having a frontier model verify, but other contributors can do that. 

Progress was slowing over the last day (relative to one new κ per minute, which is still wild for math research), but Space Bunny Max just injected fresh ideas that boosted our PR rate back to one per minute.

2) A community Lean proof of the original OpenAI Integer Multiplication paper has been completed!

@platypii et. al completed the proof in 6 days, and @0xdoug's repo is about 10–20% verified now.

To be clear, most of our work still needs verification but the Lean proofs are catching up :)

3) 41–51% of PRs now mention a prior research-only submission, up from 0–3% before @0xdoug's autoresearch.md prompt.

His prompt guides new contributors to specific research tracks rather than incremental updates.

We're moving away from "brute force research" towards more coordinated efforts across an army of agents.

If you're contributing research PRs, even negative results without a new record, you're meaningfully helping us and I appreciate it!

Interesting observations:

1) The results from free models are related to the recent "local minima" solutions in context engineering that have been popping up:

Forgetting context to "refresh" by @ShangyinT.

Branching into different solutions by @mao_yuzhen.

Fork and flush by @DimitrisPapail.

Now even free models contribute to escaping local minima by exploring new solutions, since they're trained on different data.

There's likely a lot of room for improvement now in context engineering, consensus across different models, and collaboration strategies, which we will test next.

2) Frontier research as a benchmark helped us find a successful context-sharing strategy for parallel agents.

Basically, we can rewind frontier research GitHub repos to an earlier branch and benchmark agent harnesses, prompts, context designs, models, etc.

With this benchmark, we found that you can distill constantly to local files, then periodically concatenate them instantly into parallel agent sessions to save 10–20% of the time it takes to reach the next breakthrough.

"""
Contribute one useful, independently reviewable result to https://t.co/KZP78PN7ZR. Read AGENTS.md, autoresearch.md and CONTRIBUTING.md from the current main branch first. You may post routine claims, questions, findings, handoffs and feedback in Discussions and open a focused PR without asking me again for each action. Do not merge, close others' PRs or change the selected frontier.

You can also copy this prompt into OpenCode now!

text:
What if every SaaS service could be virtualized as files? Excited to release AgentVFS and VFS-Bench 1.0 with @zechengzh: a virtual filesystem interface for AI agents, and the first systematic benchmark comparing it against MCP on the exact same tasks

One task, two interfaces: VFS v.s. MCP. 200 tasks from MCP-Atlas and Toolathlon. Every task runs once through MCP tools and once through AgentVFS, where services show up as files described by VFS.md and actions become CLIs

What we found:
- Claude Opus 5.5: 86% vs 83% pass@1, with 166k vs 617k tokens per task (73% fewer)
- GPT-6.1 Sol: same 75% success, 72% fewer tokens
- GPT-5.6 Luna: 61% → 73% success, 60% fewer tokens
- Up to 88% fewer tokens, and about 5% higher success on average

The part I find most interesting: stronger models gain the most. Opus and Sol save over 70% of their tokens, while smaller models save much less. Frontier models were post-trained heavily on terminal-style coding, and they seem to bring all of it to ls, grep, jq and pipes once you give them that interface

We spend all day building RL environments for agents. One lesson keeps coming back: the interface is part of the environment. The same task can get much easier or much harder depending on how you expose the world to the model

An AgentVFS layer may be how we scale environments for agents. One filesystem in front of every service, and the terminal skills models already have carry over to all of them
author: guohao_li
quoted_text:
We're releasing AgentVFS, a virtual filesystem interface for AI agents https://t.co/MNGMltHHvB

AgentVFS unifies every service into one interface and replaces the need of calling MCP. Stored data becomes one virtual filesystem across services, described by VFS.md, and actions become virtual CLIs, so the agent no longer calls MCP tools at all. AI agents work on live data across every service through the terminal-like interface they know best. They use the Unix tools they learned in training (ls, grep, jq, pipes, loops) and the terminal workflows they practiced in post-training on agentic coding.

We're also releasing VFS-Bench 1.0 https://t.co/TPXLRs622F, the first systematic study and benchmark to compare a virtual filesystem with MCP on the same tasks. Compared with MCP, AgentVFS uses up to 88% fewer tokens and has about a 5% higher success rate on average.

text:
OpenVLHarness is a new framework that lets multimodal LLMs *truly* use vision, search, and coding tools — and remember everything along the way.

On 22 challenging benchmarks, it boosts accuracy by 9.7–12.6 points over no-tool baselines (+11.2 for Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.9 for GPT-6 Astra). With GPT-6 Luna, it beats Codex and Visual Sketchpad at their max effort, using only 37% of their token budget.

The secret? A capability layer for consistent tool calls, plus persistent multimodal memory that stores images, arrays, and web results as reusable handles. Add a Python coding agent, and models can chain evidence, measure, search, and compute — all in a single loop.

Ablations reveal both the evidence-rendering interface and memory are essential—removing either drops 3–5 points. Automated prompt and tool optimization can add up to 8.2 points without any model fine-tuning.

As models move from lab demos to real-world visual tasks, frameworks like OpenVLHarness are closing the gap.

text:
@BlackRock filed PBIT on Monday, a Bitcoin ETF with a 10% floor.

We pulled it apart because we run a Bitcoin yield vault and wanted to know what the biggest asset manager thinks retail buyers want from protection.

Short version for anyone who doesn’t trade options on @DeriveXYZ: PBIT keeps about a third of Bitcoin’s move in both directions, loses money in most flat scenarios after fees, and the floor resets lower every month, so a slow bear market still took the structure down 28% in our backtest. 

hXXI keeps all of the Bitcoin move and adds a yield on top, paid in @HyperliquidX / @unitxyz BTC.
Over the last twenty months that has been the better trade by a wide margin, and we have the numbers.

PBIT uses three overlapping quarterly call spreads on IBIT: long the 90% strike, short a cap, remainder in bills. The cap is set wherever the sold call pays for the floor. At today’s 38% implied vol that comes out at about 13% a quarter.

It is almost insensitive to vol (12% at 23 vol and 15% at 63) because T-bill carry does most of the funding. 

We checked the model against Calamos CBXJ, the closest live product (90% floor on IBIT with a year of history). CBXJ captured 34% of IBIT’s up days and 36% of its down days.

hXXI is different. It is not forced to write calls on the full notional when the premium doesn’t cover it, and what it collects is retained in BTC.

Net of fees the factsheet shows 3.9% a year in BTC, worst month -0.9%, 17 of 20 epochs positive, max drawdown 1.8% of the Bitcoin stack. In dollars since February 2025 (IBIT -19%): NEOS income fund -17%, Roundhill covered call -24%, Innovator floor -28%.

Return per unit of volatility: hXXI is the best on the shelf, ahead of our PBIT replica, with the Calamos and Innovator floors last.

Forward we ran 20,000 paths to December 2027 at today’s implied vol with zero drift. hXXI has the highest expected return (~5%) versus under 1% for PBIT and 0% for IBIT, and the best return per unit of risk (0.11 vs PBIT’s 0.04).

PBIT does what it says in the tails: worst 5% of outcomes improve from -60% to -30%, best 5% fall from +80% to +35%.

Twenty Bitcoin buffer ETFs hold $146M total against $66B in IBIT. The largest is $25M after a year.

Option income funds hold $1.8B and every one trails $ibit. 

@JSeyff @EricBalchunas @choffstein correct us if we’re wrong, but this doesn’t sound like much demand: are IRAs confident just on BlackRock for these buffers? It’s not that complicated 😅

Twenty funds sell Bitcoin with the upside removed, on an overfitted backtest. We sell Bitcoin with more Bitcoin.

Factsheet and epoch-by-epoch record in BTC terms: DM us.
author: D2_Finance
quoted_text:
BlackRock filed a simpler copy of hXXI as an ETF.

PBIT is long $IBIT, long a put spread, and short a call to fund it.

It matches JPM’s Hedged Equity fund, which rolls the 95/80 put spread and sells the 5% OTM call quarterly on ~$20B of S&P so the call premium pays for the protection.

On $BTC at 35 vol (vs 15), a one-year 100/85 put spread costs ~6% of notional. Selling one call to fund it sets the strike near 130.

Buyers get the first 15% downside covered and keep upside to ~+30% before fees and skew. The same SPX structure caps near +18%. Crypto vol makes the collar pay nearly double.

This is the trade hXXI has run on-chain since 2025. Calls are written on only part of the notional, so most of the sleeve maintains BTC upside in spot during rallies plus delta hedging and RV trades.

Current: $1.7M TVL, 4.41% APR in BTC terms since inception, outperforming the other BTC ETF in the market.

Time to outperform Larry too.

text:
i just voted FOR reducing near:native emission to 1.6%

this is a multi-disciplinary proposal, with many implications to @NEARProtocol and its ecosystem (i'll try to address some diff implications in the next few days)

from an economics perspective: it opens doors for positioning NEAR as a strong store of value and alternative programmable money against the US dollar (and even against gold itself)

right now (October 2026):
• NEAR inflation is 2.5%
• US CPI is 3.7% (core is 2.6%)
• gold annualized supply growth is 1.5-2.0%

the target for the next 24 months:
• NEAR inflation to 1.6%
• USD inflation target by the FED is 2%
• similar expected growth rate for gold (1.5-2%)

of course, there are some nuances worth mentioning here.

according to the Austrian Economics School, inflation measures the monetary supply of a currency, not the consumer price index (CPI) increase that is a natural effect of an inflating currency (that gets diluted and loses its purchasing power over time)

but we can't really know how much the FED is printing, so the CPI is what is publicly available to measure the dollar inflation (highly prone to error, imo)

loss of purchasing power can also be affected by other factors, as, for example, with supply & demand elements related to the products and not he currency itself

the same thing is true about NEAR increase/decrease of purchasing power (or its price against the USD). supply dynamics (NEAR emission/inflation) is one factor of this equation.

the demand for NEAR (utility, speculation, etc) directly influences on whether it may or may not become a strong store of value. microeconomics (revenue, fees, burn, etc) + macroeconomics also have a high influence on that

however, supply dynamics (emission) IS STILL an important factor and it's a great step into making NEAR sound programmable money that can also act as a store of value people want to acquire, hold, stake, and use

i vote for the part that is on our control

we can't control demand part (we can create incentives for it, but not control). we can control the supply part via this proposal

i'll also support the second part of this proposal, that is upgrading my node (thecoding.pool.near) to the protocol update that will be built if this vote passes on @NEARGovernance -- as an approval on HoS will still require 80% of validators to upgrade, being the second voting round

FUN FACT: gold itself has an annual supply growth rate between 1.5-2%

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Pricing in venture is wilder than ever.

$100M pre-seed is now normal.

Bessemer just raised $1.75BN for “early” and $4BN for growth.

So can you even do seed today without $1BN?

- Is capital truly one of the last remaining moats?
- Do all small seed funds and mid-sized firms just fade into irrelevance?
- Does entry price matter anymore when there are $TRN companies…
- Is this real or a bubble that is about to burst

I sat down with @spdholakia to discuss this and have added my notes from the discussion below.

1. This Is a Supercycle Like Never Before

Sameer has spent 31 years in software and has felt magic only a handful of times. A trillion-dollar supercycle followed every one of those moments, and he notes that it does not happen very often.

What is different and what is similar to prior cycles @altcap @infoarbitrage

2. Capital Is a Moat Today

Markets pick winners and the choice becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, as it did when developers settled on SendGrid and Twilio. In legal AI, big law firms name just two major providers. Capital lets leaders scale at an extraordinary pace and build a brand, which draws talent and customers in a reinforcing flywheel.

Do you agree with this @venkyganesan @dafrankel

3. Who Wins and Who Loses in the Future of Venture Capital?

As industries professionalize, firms must be either a giant global platform that consolidates or an extreme specialist, such as an early-stage AI investor in San Francisco. Sameer counts Bessemer as a big global platform. Firms caught in between face a hard world to make money.

Is it go big or go home @rodriscoll @rabois @chetanp

4. The Rationale for Why Anthropic Would Compete With the Hyperscalers and Why We Invested

As in the cloud era, AI would be massively capital intensive, so it would consolidate to a handful of players with hundreds of apps on top. Microsoft had partnered with OpenAI and Google was building Gemini, while AWS had an undistinctive internal model and had just invested heavily in Anthropic.

5. Why Price Does Not Matter in a World of AI and the Metric That Truly Determines Value

Bessemer invested in Abridge at $5M of ARR for a $700M to $800M valuation, in Anthropic at roughly 150 times current ARR, and led Legora's $1.8B round at $20M of ARR. Sameer judges these deals on what the company can become in the next twelve months.

How has your relationship to price changed in a world of AI @mignano @mmurph

6. Why the Rise of Open Models Does Not Denigrate the Market for Closed Models

In a market this large, predicting the mix between closed and open tokens with any precision is irrelevant. Consumers, enterprises and governments will all want different flavors of intelligence. Bessemer has invested in both Anthropic and Fireworks to hold exposure to closed and open tokens.

Love to hear how you think about this @lqiao @bernhardsson

7. Why It Is a Permanent Structural Shift That Companies Will Stay Private for Longer, but Why It Will Open in 2028

With more dollars and more firms in private venture, companies will stay private longer, and most of the run-up in this boom will happen in private markets. Sameer still expects an unlock in IPOs later next year and in 2028.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @bgurley and how you see it evolving in 24 months?

we’re opening the opensea app to the public today. three big things about this launch:

social trading is now open

social trading is here, but it’s fragmented. what’s done in public on one app just lives on that app. onchain social graphs and profiles should be aggregated, open, and easy to traverse

starting today, traders from fomo, pump, and farcaster show up on opensea with their profiles and their trades in your feed. follow them, open any profile or wallet, and dig into what they’re doing. if one of those profiles is yours, import the wallet that owns it and claim it

today it’s basic aggregation. next we get smarter about what to show you, and give you more and more customization, so the most relevant trading signals rise to the top

your portfolio, your trading, and your profile in one place

today’s crypto users have balances across a few apps. you can start that way on opensea too: create a fresh wallet in a couple taps, fund it with Apple Pay, and trade without thinking about chains or wallets

but over time we think you will want more control. so we’re launching:

- track everything: link any wallet into one view and track everything you own. wallets you’ve used on opensea before link in a couple taps via web
- trade from any of it: every account comes with a wallet ready to trade. import the wallets you already use and trade coins, memes, art, trading cards
- pick what people see: choose which wallets show on your profile, set an NFT as your onchain pfp, and start creating your own native trading signals on opensea. this becomes one home for your onchain history, across every wallet and app.

trade everything, together

this is all built on top of cross-chain liquidity, real-time pricing, reliable execution, and increasing coverage for onchain assets, which we believe are tablestakes for all noncustodial consumer trading apps.

this launch: everything onchain, assets, markets, people, in one open place.

next: making it easier to trade and build together onchain. open markets, open profiles, and track records you can check, so anyone, anywhere can find each other, trust each other, and team up

text:
🧬 Virtual Embryo x Yukon 🧬

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.

author: drewcoffman
quoted_text:
When “Storm” — a seven-and-a-half-minute music video starring Swedish rapper Yung Lean and directed by Romain Gavras —  debuted in April, it seemed like a celebration of all the things AI supposedly couldn’t fake: sweat, luck, and the swagger of a guy who knows how cool he looks standing still. 

But once people started calling “Storm” something AI couldn’t do, AI companies seemed to take it personally. “The tech people were like, ‘Oh yeah? AI could never?’ Then they started replicating it,” Gavras said. “So we were forced into this conversation. It’s a nightmare.”

In September, social media was flooded with clips that re-created a half-minute from “Storm” — Lean’s cigarette, his walk up the steps, the dance explosion behind him — with the same choreography and camera moves but with Lean and his classmates replaced by strangers, pets, celebrities, and worse. Many of the clips were made with a tool called Genjutsu, which was released in late August by the AI video company Higgsfield. As the trend took off, other AI apps began offering ready-made “Storm” templates of their own.

It’s a glimpse of a future in which people can lift an artist’s style, or even their entire personality, as easily as they once downloaded mp3s. Gavras finds it “fascinating and depressing — it’s like Prometheus stealing the fire.” 

Read the full story: https://t.co/urdXx57zxb

So thrilled to meet with @Scobleizer finally in person after connecting online!

We’re excited about EVERYTHING happening now, but even more excited to imagine what the world could look like in 5, 7, or 10 years. 🤖

I believe that future will be built through software and hardware coming together. And this could be one of the most interesting places for China and the US, East and West, to connect.

This feels personal to me. I grew up in Shenzhen and watched the city grow into an entire manufacturing ecosystem. Over the past two years, seeing robotics take off on top of that supply chain has made me believe even more in hardware’s ability to connect industries, talent, and capabilities around the world.

After Telsa's showing off with new Roadster, I also keep wondering how on earth hardware can reshape consumer markets and change what people believe is possible.

Tim Cook has helped do that. @elonmusk certainly has. I keep wondering who will be next, and who that person will be in China.

What will the next major hardware platform and ecosystem look like? Robots, glasses, and wearables connected to our phones (maybe not)? Or more devices becoming part of everyone’s home and everyday life?

There’s such a huge opportunity over the next decade. These conversations leave my brain buzzing. So many possibilities, and so much still to build.

Looking forward to more conversations with Robert, and with more people thinking about AI from a global perspective. Just dm me if you are building something beyond imagination!

text:
I made a visualization of EIP-8288 aka "recursive mempool aggregation," my new favorite EIP of all time because it perfectly encapsulates the thesis of the "cryptographic world computer" -- a system whose scalability *increases*, not decreases, with the level of decentralization.

In a previous tweet I explained how EIP-8288 achieved this seemingly impossible feat, but one gif is worth a thousand words.

Essentially, EIP-8288 leverages Ethereum's decentralized mempool as a parallel ZK proving cluster.  Clients send signatures and proofs to the mempool, which over multiple rounds progressively aggregate them into fewer and fewer proofs, until the block builder finally aggregates them into one SINGLE proof.

This design accomplishes five things at once:

- The more nodes we add to the decentralized mempool, the more signatures/proofs Ethereum can process as a whole.  This is obvious if you look at the animation and imagine more nodes in the mempool ring, which would "fan out" to more signatures/proofs.

- By aggregating over multiple rounds (aka "recursive aggregation"), the bandwidth consumed by proofs remains constant for each node even as the network processes more proofs.  As a result, the network stays decentralized even as capacity increases.

- By aggregating proofs before one final aggregation by the builder, as opposed to requiring the builder to aggregate everything, the network can process more proofs without increasing hardware requirements for the builder.

- By aggregating everything to a single block-level proof, validators can verify thousands of signatures/proofs by checking just one aggregated proof.  Hardware requirements for validators can therefore stay low, keeping the network decentralized.

- By aggregating not just native signatures but also STARKs, Ethereum can support any signature scheme by wrapping them in STARKs.

So once again, this is how Ethereum will:

- scale to process tens of thousands of PQ and private transactions per second

- charge a tiny amount of gas to validate each txn, even though the original signature/proof may be huge (up to hundreds of KBs in size)

- all while decentralizing even MORE.

You are not bullish enough.
author: decentrek
quoted_text:
Ultimately, precompiles and EVM are both the wrong place to put most cryptography support into Ethereum. The reason is that precompiles and EVM both operate on data that has to be included into the ethereum chain somehow, which realistically means included in a block as calldata. That space is limited - even with PeerDAS and blocks-in-blobs, there's a practical cap of ~8 MB/s before it starts getting uncomfortable.

Remember: it's not a blockchain. It's a cryptographic world computer. Any data/computation that does not need to be in the "main thread" of data/execution should not be put into the main thread.

Instead, the correct solution is... EIP-8288 maximalism.

If you have any heavy computation that's self-contained, compute it and STARK it client-side (this is quickly getting faster and faster, even on phones), and push the STARK through the EIP-8288 recursive aggregation mechanism. The chain sees the fact that the computation was done and what the result is; it never needs to see the actual data and computation.

This way everyone can use whatever cryptography they want, the Ethereum chain can be lean, and we never need to add more precompiles again.

text:
大家以為 Google 跟 SpaceX 租算力，是 Google 自己的卡不夠、TPU 做不出來。其實照 Google 能源主管的說法，卡住的是機房還沒完全接上電。

這段話來自 CNBC 的訪談，片中沒有名牌，所以我只寫「Google 能源主管」（CNBC，@firesidealpha 轉貼，10/19）。她說，SpaceX 那份是「很短期」的合約，因為 Gemini Enterprise 客戶的需求「非常大」（同上）。

接著她講了需求有多快：一個 Gemini 產品 5 月有 4 億用戶，8 月成長到 10 億，是 Google 史上成長最快的產品（同上）。她沒有說是哪一個產品。這個用戶數我目前只看到這段影片的說法，沒有在 Google 官方資料裡找到。

再來是供給有多慢。她說 Google 正在阿肯色州的 West Memphis 蓋自有自營的資料中心，要跟當地電力公司 Entergy 合作，帶進 600MW 的新太陽能和 350MW 的新儲能（同上）。「但那需要時間」，所以「在資料中心完全接上電之前，我們有時候必須用短期方案」（同上）。

這就是整個 AI 工廠最尷尬的地方。用戶從 5 月到 8 月翻了 2.5 倍，一座電廠和併網工程卻要用年來算。就像餐廳一夜爆紅，廚房擴建要等明年，這段期間只好先跟隔壁借灶。

SpaceX 合約本身是舊消息：每月 9.2 億美元、大約 11 萬顆 GPU，2026 年底之後 90 天通知就可以解約（SEC 文件，6/5）。新的是 Google 把它定位成「很短期」，而且同一段話裡就接著講上電要時間。她沒有直接說短期方案就是指 SpaceX，但前後文很難有別的解讀。

這跟 IREN 的 Dan Roberts 說的「簽約不是瓶頸，把 GPU 上線才是」（@danroberts0101，10/19），講的是同一件事。一個是賣算力的，一個是買算力的，兩邊都說卡在上電。

也要公平說一下，能源主管講「自己付錢帶發電、幫客戶省下超過 10 億美元電費」，也有公關的成分，尤其資料中心推高電價這件事最近很敏感。

至於 SpaceX 那邊，這份合約可以 90 天通知解約，所以 Google 的電什麼時候接好，某種程度就是這份收入什麼時候結束。

全世界最會寫軟體的公司之一，現在最在意的進度條，是一條電線。

非投資建議

text:
Where there is limit there is real distinction, and where there is no limit there is none.

In the creature, matter and form are parts that together make one substance, but essence and existence are not parts at all. Essence stands in the direct line of the category, as a substance complete in its kind. Existence stands outside the substance, not as part of what it is but as the ultimate act of the whole. Essence does not join with existence to make a third thing. It receives existence, and by receiving it, it limits it. This is why the creature's being is finite and really distinct from what the creature is.

In God nothing is received, so nothing is limited, and among His perfections there is no real or formal distinction at all. In creatures, perfections are formally distinct because each is confined to being itself and not another. In God they are united in a higher order, as the sun's light holds the power to warm and the power to dry in one nature. His intellect and will act as though they were distinct, but their distinction is only virtual, contained eminently in His one unlimited perfection.

Bl. Dun Scotus puts a formal distinction into God and so brings limit where there is none, whereas Suárez removes the real distinction from the creature and so leaves its limit without a ground. Both fail on the ground that act is limited only by what receives it.

市场还在问AI算力是不是建多了，老马在电话会上报了个数：今年剩下的时间，每个月上线约20万颗英伟达GB300。明年还要保持类似速度，主要换成Vera Rubin。$SPCX $NVDA 

按他的计划，今年底上线2.5–3GW算力，2027年再增加约10GW，年底做到约13GW。另外，明年二季度末，要让一个拥有44万颗Vera Rubin GPU的训练集群投入运行。

这也解释了为什么他最近老往孟菲斯跑。他说自己经常一周在那里待四天，白天黑夜都在盯。卡买回来之后，电接不上、冷却跟不上，一样没法用，所以明年还计划新增20GW的供电和冷却基础设施，给后面的GPU部署提前留位置。

text:
Matter Labs announced that ZKsync EraVM is being retired, with the legacy execution environment entering its end-of-life. 

[[ New Viacoin Via on public testnet, is built on ZKsync Era ]] 

Its successor, ZKsync OS introduces a fundamentally different architecture. A new Rust-based state-transition implementation, compiled for native execution in the sequencer & RISC-V execution for zero-knowledge proving through “Airbender”

Given that upstream development is moving to this new architecture, I've decided Via will follow. Well, I have to. There's not much of a choice.  

ZKsync's Security Council also disclosed several preventative security upgrades addressing more than 5 vulnerabilities in legacy EraVM proving system, including circuit soundness & cryptographic weaknesses.

Which (unfortunately or fortunately depending on who you ask) further reinforces the need to reassess Via's current architecture before mainnet.

It's not a straightforward version upgrade. Large parts of Via's current implementation need to be replaced or adapted, especially where Via's custom Bitcoin settlement, data availability & proving infrastructure interact with the execution layer. This will require asubstantial engineering work.

Overall, I do believe following upstream (zksync) now will pay off, rather than just kicking the can further down the road

The development and Via's repositories and work (except infra) is open-source available and you can track development if you're curious 

Staying in sync with upstream is painful, death by thousand merge conflicts. The original Viacoin was based on Bitcoin, getting in sync 2016-2018 often meant reforking Bitcoin and implementing every Bitcoin feature.

This is a similar scenario where I have to fork Zksync it's new OS repository. Reimplement every Viacoin/Via v2 feature. 

I've been doing researching how established projects maintain large upstream forks. How Brave stays synchronized with Chromium. Asking Claude pls isn't going to cut it. Maybe one day. 

There are engineering practices I can adopt. Isolating downstream modifications, maintaining auditable patch sets, automating upstream change detection & reducing the cost of future upgrades. It's probably one of the most sophisticated strategy I've seen, it's impressive. They're also working on an experimental tool called “Plaster” which allows brave to apply changes to upstream source files by relying on regex transformations to search for patterns and apply substitutions. 

The goal is not just to migrate Via to ZKsync OS, but to establish a more structurally maintainable architecture & a better process for staying synchronized with upstream going forward 

I am in a state of tired boss and also super excited. Zksync new tech is incredibly exciting

Dude shit it feels like Dyson released a new vacuum and it will be delivered soon kinda excited  

I know for most this post won't be important and lots of you don't even know I have a project while others may remember Viacoin back in 2016/2017 or the newer Via v2 announcement

Here’s what we know so far about GTA 6’s mission structure. Based on trailers, leaks, and the information we’ve been able to piece together, we were able to get a pretty clear picture of how the missions could stack up, from the most important story missions to optional side content:

▫️ "Diner Robbery" - First major heist establishing Jason and Lucia's partnership
▫️ "Doggy to the moon, Dumbass" - Crypto shitcoin scam mission with massive payout potential
▫️ "Vice City Bank Heist" - Central story mission advancing their criminal empire
▫️ "FIB Files" - Key mission where they steal incriminating evidence
▫️ "Port Authority Takeover" - Critical for controlling smuggling operations
▫️ "Drug Empire" - Major story mission establishing narcotics network
▫️ "Yacht Hijack" - High-stakes heist on the waters of Vice City
▫️ "Airport Contraband" - Intercepting weapons shipment crucial for story progression
▫️ "Witness Protection" - Eliminating key witnesses before testimony
▫️ "Cypress Creek Cartel" - Taking down rival operations in the swamps
▫️ "Prison Break" - Springing a high-value ally from maximum security
▫️ "Leonida Takeover" - Final mission establishing control over the state
▫️ "Club Takeover" - Establishing control of Vice City's nightlife
▫️ "Biker War" - Settling territorial disputes with motorcycle clubs
▫️ "Gator Hunt" - Dangerous pursuit through the Everglades
▫️ "Mall Mayhem" - Hostage situation in luxury shopping center
▫️ "Junkyard Justice" - Settling scores in the industrial district
▫️ "Vice Beach Rumble" - Turf war with the beach gangs
▫️ "Dock Wars" - Fighting for control of shipping industry
▫️ "Recon Mission" - Gathering intel on rival operations
▫️ "Snatch & Grab" - Quick kidnapping for ransom
▫️ "Courier Service" - Running packages for various contacts
▫️ "Repo Man" - Collecting on delinquent payments
▫️ "Vigilante Justice" - Taking out low-level criminals for cash
▫️ "Taxi Driver" - Undercover transport operations
▫️ "Beach Patrol" - Security work for wealthy beach residents
▫️ "Food Delivery" - Front for smuggling operations
▫️ "Limo Service" - Chauffeuring high-profile clients

The picture we were able to put together shows a clear progression, starting with Lucia's prison release and moving into increasingly complex heists, criminal operations, and territory takeovers.

The main story also appears to be shorter than RDR2, while still having a huge amount of side content and optional activities.

text:
This is total nonsense.

We're one of the largest early investors in Polymarket, and this story that Shayne was "caught red-handed" using company money is just a flat out garbage hit piece.

Shayne wasn't taking a salary. He was 21 when he started Polymarket, he was living hand-to-mouth running the company out of his apartment, barely making ends meet when he was raising his seed round. We were his first term sheet and literally offered to loan him money personally, but he ended up not needing it when the seed round came together.

After COVID and the crazy Biden-era crackdown on crypto that was happening at the time, there was a lot of chaos in almost every company in the industry. As an investor, we saw a lot of companies go through pandemic-era startup craziness, and Polymarket was no exception.

But Shayne disclosed every dollar he spent, which turned out to annualize to about a software engineer's salary. That's including the flights, none of which were personal flights. Plus, SHAYNE STARTED the accounting and payback process, no one “found” it. In aggregate, it was nothing that an investor would balk at. He paid it back to the company in full, and then got on a normal salary like everyone else.

It was an accounting problem, not an integrity problem. It was not a big deal.

Polymarket has had growing pains, no doubt. It went from a small fledging startups to one of the most explosive consumer brands in America. But Shayne has leveled up alongside the company, and as investors we have total confidence in him.

text:
Everyone keeps asking if the AI bubble pops soon. I don't think it pops before the OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs, and that's why Worldcoin is on my watchlist.

Yes, we're in an AI bubble. Of course we are. But saying it pops right now because things are expensive isn't a plan. Things can get more expensive.

Here's my logic. If AI stocks crash as hard as people say, they can't be back at all-time highs two months later. That doesn't happen. And these IPOs need a hot market, with the Nasdaq near its highs.

Only one of those can be true.

Think about who gets paid. The banks underwriting these deals and the exchanges taking them public make their money from these two final IPOs. So I don't see them letting the market melt down before then. As long as the OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs haven't happened, I don't think we get an AI meltdown.

Don't bet on the bubble popping until all the liquidity has been extracted.

Now Worldcoin. It's co-founded by Sam Altman, and it's doing weird stuff again. To me that says it's warming up its buzz ahead of the OpenAI IPO.

I've been playing with this idea a lot. Worldcoin could be the higher-beta bet on the OpenAI IPO, with more volatility than OpenAI itself. And the trade has clear bounds. The IPO is the catalyst, and you want to be out before it happens.

So once the OpenAI IPO date is locked in, I'd be interested in trading Worldcoin and selling it shortly before the IPO date. We don't know that date yet.

Right now it's only on my watchlist. I don't hold it

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger on the manufacturing bottleneck between designing hardware with AI and actually getting it built:

"Let's say we're off to do a great new chip together, the one that's gonna leap ahead because we have understanding of the AI workloads... And let's say we turn our AI tools loose. Within three months we have an awesome design."

"[But] we still have like a couple of really major bottlenecks today. One is we still have nine months of silicon processing time... So I can design the thing in three months, but I can't actually get it into real silicon at scale for nine months."

"We have to really see that bottleneck improve if we're gonna have this innovation."

"If it takes me a year and a half until I actually get scale and software on it, my understanding of the AI workloads is no longer applicable to the chip that I designed."

know ive been tweeting about this a lot but really think papertrade could be a generational setup

high leverage perps are crypto's most profitable product to date, demand for speculation is not going to go away

ability to open/close synthetic 1000x positions w/ no market impact is a novel mechanism, paired w/ the house-trader relationship where trader losses fund the onchain LP, & all losses after a certain LP cap get paid out to traders staking the platform's native paper token - can see how this can maintain traction longterm, already at 50M+ paid out to $PAPER stakers in first week

every other perp dex's revenue comes from a small take rate on the fees of volume, no perp dex has been able to monetize directly trader losses, of which it's been shown is a much larger number, in theory winners should be able to easily get paid out from house LP over time as high leverage has a difficult success rate, ideal state is that its closer to 50/50 winners/losers after a certain LP cap and even then its a much better model allowing traders to own the house

what's more interesting tho is that the model should be able to be extensible to other games outside of just perpetual futures, the online gambling industry is massive, and none of the online casinos are +EV for users, every major online casino is -EV as thats how the house makes money by creating games that are slightly better probabilistically for the house and monetizing losses over time, with papertrade it should be possible to let people speculate on other similar games with the same model as losses going back directly to paper stakers instead of just to the house - so im curious to see what team is thinking of here

if hyperliquid is the AWS of all of finance, then papertrade could be the AWS of all high leverage speculation money games on the internet, will be cool to see how the next several months play out, dont think people have gone deep enough on the possibilities with one of the first novel onchain experiments in awhile that also rewards its most active participants

SITUATION EXPLAINED: For the first time, AI-designed viruses were given to a human patient to fight a drug-resistant infection.

• The viruses are bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria, designed by Omnii-1, a genome language model from Radical Numerics, a startup founded by members of the Arc Institute's Evo team
• The patient's E. coli infection resisted antibiotics and every available phage
• Omnii-1 redesigned the "legs" phages use to grab bacteria, and a cocktail of the new variants wiped out the patient's bacteria in a lab dish
• The cocktail then went to the patient under compassionate use, but the outcome hasn't been shared, citing privacy
• Antibiotic resistance could cause nearly 40M deaths by 2050, and finding the right phage by hand can take months

@theojaffee: "A virus is barely alive. You can just think of them as sort of tiny self-replicators. It literally repurposes the internal machinery of the bacterial cell to make more of itself, and it manufactures so many viruses, the cell will burst, which kills the bacteria."

text:
this California wealth tax thing is just incredible. 

so in October 2025, a California healthcare union proposed a "one time" 5% tax on any billionaire's wealth. the ballot measure will be voted on next month. In early December 2025, California announced that it would be a retroactive tax if passed, applying to anyone with CA residency as of Jan 1, 2026. The objective is to pay for Medi-Cal, California's incredibly dysfunctional healthcare system. (which also functions as a glorified welfare apparatus, but that's a discussion for another time). 

polls reveal that the CA electorate is split around 50/50 on the tax, but prediction markets only give Prop 40 a ~23% chance of passing (there are competing measures on the ballet that would nullify it). 

there are 200 billionaires in CA, worth collectively somewhere between $2.3 and $2.6 trillion. 5% of that is around $100b, accounting for a small amount of attrition. proponents of the tax forecasted a significant windfall, assuming only a 10% departure rate. 

supporters thought they were being clever with the retroactive concept. no billionares would leave CA in the few short months between the tax being proposed and the residency cutoff date, without the tax even having passed yet, right? 

well as it turns out, they did. 

a new paper [1] from two academics at Stanford called "The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act", argues that not only did more billionaires leave due to the proposed tax than its proponents expected, but that the value of the tax, if it does pass, is actually negative. 

proponents of the tax only assumed 10% avoidance, that is, only 10% of the taxable base of targeted billionaires would leave CA within the very short Oct-Dec 2025 window. Jaros and Rauh, the Stanford academics, find that a lower bound of 28.6% of the taxable base managed to leave. 

just based on known departures, those departures total $577b in net worth, or $28.8b in potential tax lost. this of course does not capture everyone (many left without announcing their departure), so the authors normalize to departure rates estimated from other wealth tax events, and apply other discounts for litigation, arriving arrive at a figure of only $28-$36b in forecasted tax revenues. 

but this isn't all! all of the income taxes paid by the departed billionaires are also forsaken. the authors estimate that CA billionaires pay $3.3- 5.8b in annual income taxes. they assume a midpoint of $2b lost in annual collections from departed billionaires. the net present value of that lost income stream is -$68.9 billion. 

so when you add it all up you get: 

+ $30b one-time tax windfall (estimated)  
- $69b in present value of lost future income taxes
= - 38.9b overall net present value of the tax 

of course, this analysis is highly estimate driven. the authors simulate the parameters 100k times and find a negative NPV of the implemented tax 85 percent of the time. 

and if the tax doesn't pass, which it's not looking like it will, California still ended up losing at least $577b in departed net worth, and they have permanently poisoned the well with entrepreneurs who will now worry about future wealth taxes. 

[1]: https://t.co/1lbZgnMTG9
