text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

text:
1986年，拉斯维加斯每家赌场联手封杀了同一个人。  

他们以为故事到此结束。  

结果这人揣着18万美元飞到香港，开始赌马。    

最后几乎赚了9亿美元  

他叫 Bill Benter。  

赌场封杀他，是因为他算牌。  

到了马场，他干了一模一样的事:  

只是把扑克牌换成了马。

他的全部秘密，浓缩成一行公式：  

EV = p · b − (1 − p)  

p 是你算出的真实胜率，b 是赔率。 

EV 大于零，押。
小于零，走人。没有第三种情况。  

他花了好几年，喂给电脑几十个变量: 骑师体重、赛道湿度、马的血统、历史跑位: 只为把每匹马的真实胜率算到比庄家更准。  

庄家定价偏了，他就吃这个价差。  

庄家没偏，他一分钱不碰。  

这段 45 分钟的 MIT 概率公开课，讲的就是这件事。  

华尔街量化交易员、职业赌徒、对冲基金分析师的共同起点。  

MIT 学生一年交 8 万美金来听。 

现在免费摆在网上。  

Benter 没有内幕，没有运气，没有神秘系统。  

他只是认真做了数学作业。  

绝大多数人在"感觉会赢"的时候下注。 

真正赚到钱的人，只在数学说"值得"的时候出手。  

区别只有一个： 你下注前，有没有先算 EV。 https://t.co/6qi7S8ImP6

马斯克由于利益冲突不能参与讨论，但他认为两家的协同（超级智能软件、芯片设计、Terafab 芯片工厂、机器人、入轨运载…）会有很大收益

全文稿：

这个问题让我感觉像在雷区里跳踢踏舞，所以我得谨慎斟酌在这里说的话。

SpaceX 和特斯拉都已应股东要求成立了特别委员会，来讨论这个想法。这些特别委员会由独立董事组成。而因为我是利益冲突方，我实际上不能参与特别委员会的讨论。所以这有点像一场奇怪的歌舞伎表演：两拨人在谈，而我却不能参与其中。

我认为我们不应该想当然。外界有些人认为 SpaceX 和特斯拉合并是板上钉钉的事，我认为这种说法言过其实了。

那么，我认为这是个好主意吗？是的。但归根结底，股东必须支持这件事。尤其是特斯拉这边，我们需要全部股份 50% 的赞成票——不只是参与投票的，而是全体股东。这是一个相当高的门槛。

我只能说，目前为止，特别委员会尚未就任何交易条款达成一致，而且显然也无法保证他们一定会达成。

但我确实认为合并两家公司有很多好处，因为我们基本已处于超级智能奇点。在超级智能软件、芯片设计、Terafab 芯片工厂、机器人，以及借助星链星座连接能力的入轨运载等领域合作开发，会有很大收益。

所以我认为这会是个好主意，但这真的取决于两家公司的特别委员会。他们得先拿出一个方案，然后再提交股东投票表决。

pretty interesting experiment from Bayes Market: 

basically they're connecting prediction markets that are related to each other instead of treating every bet separately.

say Nvidia beating earnings jumps from 40% to 80%.

then that new information should also affect markets like AI chip demand or data center spending.

Bayes Market uses these relationships to estimate how the odds in other markets should change.

the opportunity is spotting markets that haven't reacted yet and trading the difference before prices catch up.

could get even more interesting with AI agents constantly monitoring thousands of connected markets and finding mispricings automatically. 

still experimental but pretty cool mechanism.

text:
$TORCH 14.6m dyor

0x000050e18ffa3f8f7ad170eb9cef160eb3ed1111

okx wallet:https://t.co/TVOhrFHGgB

A multi-chain trading + token launch platform, focused on "one balance, cross-chain operations."

It integrates a trading terminal, a Telegram trading bot, and a fair launchpad. The core idea: users can use just one balance to buy and sell tokens across multiple chains, launch new tokens, and trade cross-chain—without manually moving funds around or managing a bunch of wallets.

The core pain points the project aims to solve:

Multi-chain trading is too much hassle.

Traditional launchpads are prone to "liquidity pulls" or team rug pulls.

Most launchpads are just "extraction"—creators take their fees and leave, with no ongoing rewards for holders.

The full memecoin cycle is too fragmented.

So Torch wants to put this entire loop into one platform.

The product currently has three main components:

Terminal: token discovery, trading, limit orders, take-profit/stop-loss, portfolio tracking, Alpha feed, and token launches.

Telegram Bot: paste a contract address to quickly buy/sell, set take-profit/stop-loss, bridge, etc.

Launchpad: one-click token launches on Robinhood Chain.

Features:

At launch, 100% of the supply goes directly into a Uniswap v4 pool, with liquidity permanently locked.

No bonding curve, no migration.

Configurable buy tax (creator 70% / protocol 30%). Creators can choose to keep the money for themselves, use it for buybacks and burns, or distribute it to holders.

Multi-chain support.

TORCH is the platform token, with the main functions:

Value capture: a portion of platform trading fees and launch-related revenue flows back to holders.

Burn mechanism: trading triggers buybacks and burns of the token, continuously reducing supply.

Pairing asset: new tokens can be launched paired with TORCH.

Holder returns:
70% of the 2% buy tax goes to holders (in the early stage, most of this is used for buybacks and burns).
About 25% of net platform revenue is also distributed to holders based on their holdings.

Jeff 的 handle @chameleon_jeff ，第一个词代表 Chameleon Trading，是 Jeff 离职 HRT 后创办的加密量化交易公司，也是 Hyperliquid 前身。

Jeff 靠 1 万美金本金起家，靠量化做市策略赚出创业第一桶金。FTX 倒闭后停掉量化交易业务，转向自建去中心化永续合约交易所，于是我们有了 Hyperliquid。而 Chameleon Trading 沉淀下来的成功经验和策略，最终沉淀成了 HLP vault。

一切都能连起来。

一套量化策略 - 一个基金结构 - 一个链上金库，有没有很熟悉？

OpenETF 就是这套基建的 HyperEVM 版本。

过去几年跟不少成熟的量化团队有过接触，好的策略往往不对外募资，基本都是自营。但时代正在变。

加密市场的开放 API 和云基础设施（AWS 等）让个人/小团队也能触及与传统金融机构类似的流动性池，这与传统 HFT 需要巨额基础设施形成鲜明对比。

此外 AI 的加持进一步放大个人交易者的生产力，量化交易可以被更广泛应用。

1 万美金的传奇不多见，毕竟那是 Jeff。但对于小型量化团队、量化 OPC 而言，本金依然是重要的生产要素。

OpenETF 省掉传统基金结构冗余的成本，提供了一个公开、透明、可验证的链上基金结构。你只需要创建一支 quant ETF，然后交易。

你系统代表 ETF 交易，但无法转出其他投资人的资金，链上代码写死。只需要专注交易，用链上业绩说话，赢得投资人用 USDC 给你投票。

你的量化系统就是一支基金。
build your own "Chameleon", the ETF way.

考虑到 HL 原生 API 可以交易任何 HL 上的资产，包括流动性极差的资产，出于保护投资人利益的目的，首个版本不对开放 HL 原生 API，可能无法满足 HFT 高频量化策略的需求。后续会逐步放开。

OpenETF 在内测收口阶段，Private Beta 即将跟大家见面，Genesis Pass 持有者可以参与测试。

ETF everything.

author: BessemerVP
quoted_text:
Pricing in venture is wilder than ever.

$100M pre-seed is now normal.

Bessemer just raised $1.75BN for “early” and $4BN for growth.

So can you even do seed today without $1BN?

- Is capital truly one of the last remaining moats?
- Do all small seed funds and mid-sized firms just fade into irrelevance?
- Does entry price matter anymore when there are $TRN companies…
- Is this real or a bubble that is about to burst

I sat down with @spdholakia to discuss this and have added my notes from the discussion below.

1. This Is a Supercycle Like Never Before

Sameer has spent 31 years in software and has felt magic only a handful of times. A trillion-dollar supercycle followed every one of those moments, and he notes that it does not happen very often.

What is different and what is similar to prior cycles @altcap @infoarbitrage

2. Capital Is a Moat Today

Markets pick winners and the choice becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, as it did when developers settled on SendGrid and Twilio. In legal AI, big law firms name just two major providers. Capital lets leaders scale at an extraordinary pace and build a brand, which draws talent and customers in a reinforcing flywheel.

Do you agree with this @venkyganesan @dafrankel

3. Who Wins and Who Loses in the Future of Venture Capital?

As industries professionalize, firms must be either a giant global platform that consolidates or an extreme specialist, such as an early-stage AI investor in San Francisco. Sameer counts Bessemer as a big global platform. Firms caught in between face a hard world to make money.

Is it go big or go home @rodriscoll @rabois @chetanp

4. The Rationale for Why Anthropic Would Compete With the Hyperscalers and Why We Invested

As in the cloud era, AI would be massively capital intensive, so it would consolidate to a handful of players with hundreds of apps on top. Microsoft had partnered with OpenAI and Google was building Gemini, while AWS had an undistinctive internal model and had just invested heavily in Anthropic.

5. Why Price Does Not Matter in a World of AI and the Metric That Truly Determines Value

Bessemer invested in Abridge at $5M of ARR for a $700M to $800M valuation, in Anthropic at roughly 150 times current ARR, and led Legora's $1.8B round at $20M of ARR. Sameer judges these deals on what the company can become in the next twelve months.

How has your relationship to price changed in a world of AI @mignano @mmurph

6. Why the Rise of Open Models Does Not Denigrate the Market for Closed Models

In a market this large, predicting the mix between closed and open tokens with any precision is irrelevant. Consumers, enterprises and governments will all want different flavors of intelligence. Bessemer has invested in both Anthropic and Fireworks to hold exposure to closed and open tokens.

Love to hear how you think about this @lqiao @bernhardsson

7. Why It Is a Permanent Structural Shift That Companies Will Stay Private for Longer, but Why It Will Open in 2028

With more dollars and more firms in private venture, companies will stay private longer, and most of the run-up in this boom will happen in private markets. Sameer still expects an unlock in IPOs later next year and in 2028.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @bgurley and how you see it evolving in 24 months?

之前在新加坡，正好撞见了 GRVT 的 DB，和他聊了不少项目未来的规划。没想到这么快，GRVT 就正式公布了接下来六周的重大产品更新计划。

看了一下，这次更新的东西还真不少，基本上是要把交易、理财和投资整合到一个账户里。接下来有四个值得关注的更新：

1. Grvt Earn（10月底）

推出全新的收益产品，将传统金融的固定收益资产引入链上，储蓄产品目标年化收益最高可达 11%，收益来源包括利息、保费和应收账款等真实资产现金流。

2. Stable Funding Perps（11月）

这是我比较关注的产品。GRVT 准备把股票、外汇、商品、指数等 TradFi 资产整合到同一个账户，提供零交易手续费、更稳定的资金费率，以及更好的交易深度。
按照官方规划，到12月底支持的交易标的将超过1000个。

3. Yield as Margin（11月）

这个功能挺有意思，用户可以直接把 Earn 账户中的生息资产作为交易保证金。也就是说，你的资金一边可以赚取理财收益，一边还能作为保证金参与交易。对于经常交易的用户来说，资金利用率会高很多。当然，理财收益不代表交易保证金没有风险。

4. Grvt 2.0（11月底）

全新品牌形象和重新设计的 App，整合以上全部功能。

说完产品，再聊聊 ethereum:0xad29f2723fcdbcf665f210f25e06f97477e417cf，我感觉接下来可能会有一波值得关注的看涨机会。原因主要有两个：

首先是代币回购和销毁。GRVT 已经完成首轮公开市场回购，累计回购并销毁了110万枚 ethereum:0xad29f2723fcdbcf665f210f25e06f97477e417cf，接近当前流通供应量的1%。

其次，也是我更看重的一点：新产品能不能真正带来新的用户和收入。过去的 GRVT 主要围绕加密资产交易展开，而接下来，它要同时切入 TradFi 交易和链上理财市场。

一旦 Earn 能够吸引更多资金沉淀，TradFi 产品带来新的交易用户，再通过生息保证金提高资金利用率，就有机会形成一个正向循环。当然，这个逻辑成立的前提是产品如期上线，并且真的有用户愿意使用。

接下来六周，我会重点关注它的新产品上线情况，以及真实用户和收入数据。@grvt_io

author: sreeramkannan
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

text:
Spent the last two weeks in SF and NYC talking to AI native law firms, GCs and academics. Here are my observations:

1. Part of the AI native law firm thesis is to build proprietary software that beats Harvey/Legora. But their most cracked lawyers that I have talked to won't even use the internal tool. They prefer their own harness on Claude Code or Codex. 

2. Some people are convinced that certain AI native law firms were built just to become RL environments that generate real dataset for the labs. 

3. Ex-BigLaw lawyers at AI natives miss working on headline deals (the ones that get you into Legal500 and Chambers & Partners).

4. BigLaw made its money running billion-dollar cross-border deals with multiple parties that agents can't run unsupervised. No AI native firm is doing that sort of work. BigLaw solved it by sorting out multi-jurisdictional licensing and regulatory issues across offices, with precise staffing.  AI can potentially do the staffing part really well, but not the licensing part.

5. No AI native firm has a hiring strategy for 10x lawyers. They prefer hiring partners as their salesforce. The best 10x lawyers I know are still in BigLaw. AI natives need software-like margins so they focus on commoditized work that a model + purpose built harness can finish autonomously. And 10x lawyers enjoy doing non-routine, non-automatable tasks in the fastest way possible using AI. 

6. The next frontier, if I am right, is full stack lawyers, lawyers who spot a new area of emerging practice and build productized service around that to monopolize a segment quickly (essentially turn your advice into an API that clients can run by BYOA). It's cheaper and easier than hiring partners to buy their client relationships. Specialist practices like tax, ERISA and regulatory have best chance of winning here.

author: soubhikdeb
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

text:
OpenAI 买了一家 AI 药企，但不是设计分子的环节

OpenAI 收购了 Orchestra Bio，并进自家的生命科学项目 Rosalind。
这家公司不碰分子生成，做的事看着很传统：用 AI Agent 帮药企盯试验排期、临床进度，协调生产延误。

官方公告里说：一款新药，平均还要走 10 到 15 年。
大模型公司进医药，最先吃下的不是科学，是运营。

1、团队什么来头

CEO Ashoka Rajendra，Benchling 前开发与生产产品负责人。
- Benchling 是生物医药研发软件的龙头，2021 年 F 轮估值 61 亿美元，官方称有 1300 多家生物技术公司在用，包括默克、Moderna、赛诺菲，用来记实验、管样本和数据。
- 他做的正是药从实验室走向生产那一段的软件。药企在哪脱节、在哪漏钱，他看得最清楚。

CTO Andy Xu，Numenta 前工程副总裁。
- Numenta 是 Palm 创始人 Jeff Hawkins 2005 年创办的公司，从脑科学出发做 AI，后来主攻让模型推理更快、更省，官方称能把推理提速 10 到 100 倍以上。
- 排期和调度这种活，每天要跑大量推理，成本压不下来就用不起。

一个懂药企流程，一个懂把系统跑便宜。

2、瓶颈不在算法

分子设计热闹了好几年，大家以为 AI 能很快算出新药。
但算出来之后，合成、动物实验、三期临床，一步都省不掉。
物理世界的试错，算法替不了。

3、科学决定上限，脏活决定死活

新药研发的时间，大量耗在内部摩擦上：部门沟通脱节，外包研究机构排期延误，放大生产时断档。
把从发现到临床之间这层信息断层理顺，Agent 现在就能省出真金白银。

我觉得 OpenAI 这笔投资要的还有入口和数据。
只跑分子模型的工具，很难进药企的核心决策；接管了临床和生产的调度，药企每天真实的工作流数据，就从它这里过。

4、先啃流程脏活，再图科学圣杯。

分子设计卖的是十几年后的彩票。
流程协调卖的是明天的现金账本。

大家以为大模型进药企会先当爱因斯坦，结果它先去当了项目经理。

text:
Extraction models turn human language into data your software can act on. We're bringing them to Sage. 

Early access tomorrow for everyone who registers on @levantolabs by  PT today. Demo 📺👇

Most software needs structured inputs. People communicate through emails, chats, tickets, contracts, and conversations.

Extraction models connect those two interfaces. You define the information your application needs, and the model identifies it in the text: people, companies, products, dates, amounts, descriptions, or requests.

Calling this “extracting stuff from documents” understates what developers can build with it.

Consider a customer message:

“The blue jacket arrived with a broken zip. Please send a replacement to 18 King Street.”

An extraction model can identify the product, defect, requested remedy, and address. Your application now has fields it can validate, look up, and pass to a tool.

A decision model can then evaluate whether the request qualifies for an automatic replacement, needs more information, or requires human review.

Extraction → decision → action.

Each stage has a defined responsibility. Extraction supplies the values. The decision model evaluates the available options against your policy and context. Your application validates the result and controls execution.

That separation matters for agent builders. You can inspect what the model extracted, test the decision independently, and control which actions are permitted.

Speed changes where this becomes useful.

At roughly 200 ms for extraction, developers can start putting language interpretation directly into interactive software:

• A support interface that fills relevant fields while an agent reads a ticket.
• A browser agent that extracts values from a message before populating a form.
• A find-in-page feature that highlights cancellation deadlines or product complaints, even when the text uses different wording.
• A workflow that turns an incoming email into validated tool arguments and evaluates the next action.

The opportunity extends to any application where someone currently reads a message, copies information into fields, and decides what happens next.

Developers can define the information they need and the decisions their software must make, then connect those outputs to existing functions.

We're bringing extraction and decision models together in Sage so builders can implement that flow.

text:
I believe $DACITY is one of the GTA VI-related Memes worth continuing to watch right now.

nxPqZ4F7ux8Vph5NFu25rEP6Kx9Gr1U6Fmj36Rjpump 

The reason is not simply that it has attached itself to the massive GTA VI IP.

It's that it has a real content anchor behind it: a pink stunt plane bearing the DacityCoin name appeared in Rockstar's official trailer.

This is quite different from most gaming-themed concept coins. The narratives behind many tokens come from community speculation, leaks, or artificially constructed associations. Once a new market hot topic emerges, they can easily be replaced. But DacityCoin, which DACITY is associated with, is itself a fictional element in the GTA VI game world. Players can see it in the game, streamers may discover it while playing, and creators can produce clips and Memes around this detail.

I think this is what makes it genuinely worth researching: it has the opportunity to benefit from GTA VI's own content distribution rather than relying solely on narrative cycles within the crypto community.

Of course, Rockstar featuring DacityCoin in the game does not mean it endorses the on-chain DACITY. The relationship between the two is a connection through content and narrative, not an official partnership. To me, this distinction does not weaken its potential as a Meme, because my bet has never been on whether Rockstar will endorse the token. It is on whether this fictional brand in the game can continue attracting attention and eventually spread into the crypto market.

Looking at its previous price action, DACITY has already demonstrated strong event-driven characteristics. When the related footage began circulating, the token started a rally. After the release of the official GTA VI trailer, DacityCoin attracted market attention again, and its market cap surged into the millions of dollars. This at least shows that when a specific element from a game enters the public eye, the market is willing to build a trading narrative around it.

But one rally can only prove that it is capable of capturing attention, not that this attention can be sustained. For me, the next important question is what happens after GTA VI officially launches.

The currently announced release date is November 19, 2026. Once the game reaches players, DacityCoin could experience a second wave of distribution that differs from the attention generated by the trailer: players discover the relevant element in the game, streamers showcase it during livestreams, gameplay clips get edited and shared on social media, and more people who previously had no interest in crypto begin discussing the name. If this process actually happens, DACITY could gain another wave of attention from the gaming community rather than repeatedly relying on the same group of crypto traders trading among themselves.

I believe that when a Meme is connected to a major gaming IP, its ability to continuously generate content is what matters most. An ordinary crypto news story can quickly be replaced by the next one, but a game with a massive player base can continuously generate gameplay streams, Easter egg discoveries, mission discussions, and fan-created content. As long as DacityCoin is presented prominently enough in the game, it has a chance to become part of that content.

Of course, the game's release does not automatically mean the token will rise. Players may be interested in the game without caring about the on-chain DACITY at all. The market may also price in expectations ahead of the release and choose to take profits when the event actually happens. Therefore, what I want to observe is whether genuinely new buyers appear before and after the launch, whether game-related content continues to spread, and whether trading activity can evolve from a short-lived burst into more sustained demand.

Another noteworthy design choice is that DACITY uses TTWO as its trading pair. TTWO is associated with Take-Two Interactive, and Take-Two is the parent company of Rockstar. From a narrative perspective, this pairing fits the GTA VI theme better than an arbitrary trading pair, connecting the token's trading structure to the commercial ecosystem behind the game. However, this remains an association at the narrative and trading-structure level. It does not mean that DACITY has been endorsed by Take-Two or Rockstar, nor does holding DACITY give holders equity exposure to TTWO.

Holder rewards are another supplementary feature. According to the interface I saw, 0.05% of every transaction's Creator Fee is used to distribute TTWO to eligible holders. The minimum holding requirement is $20 worth of tokens, and rewards are distributed proportionally to holdings. The page recorded approximately 36.8 TTWO in cumulative distributions and around 56,900 distribution payments.

This mechanism has actual distribution records, meaning holders have an opportunity to receive additional TTWO rewards beyond price appreciation. However, I would not consider it a powerful value-capture mechanism simply because it exists. The 0.05% fee rate is low, and the rewards must be distributed among eligible wallets. It is more like an additional incentive for holding than a core factor determining DACITY's long-term valuation.

What I care about more is whether trading demand can expand as GTA VI-related content gains new exposure. If trading volume growth merely reflects turnover among existing traders, even continuous reward distributions may not be enough to support a higher valuation. Conversely, if the game keeps attracting new users and liquidity and buying demand can keep pace, holder rewards may become more meaningful as the overall trading ecosystem grows.

Additionally, the project interface shows that developer holdings are at 0% and that Mint and Freeze authorities have been renounced. These are worth noting as positive supporting signals. They can reduce some concerns about the developer's ability to directly mint additional tokens or freeze them, but they do not mean the token is free of other risks. Related wallets, the actual distribution of holdings, and liquidity conditions still need to be assessed independently.

I would not assign DACITY an attractive-looking market cap target simply because GTA VI has a massive player base. What really matters is not how many players the game has, but how many of them will encounter DacityCoin, how much of the related content can spread beyond the gaming community, and how much of that attention ultimately translates into genuine token demand. The scale of the gaming IP creates an opportunity for distribution, but it does not directly determine the token's valuation ceiling.

Therefore, my bullish thesis on DACITY is clear for now: it has a narrative directly anchored to official GTA VI content, and the November 19 release provides a new window for attention. The TTWO pairing and holder rewards give it some additional differentiation, but what will truly determine its future upside is whether DacityCoin can be repeatedly discovered, discussed, and shared by players after the game launches, and whether that exposure can translate into sustained market demand.

To me, what makes DACITY most worth betting on is not the rally that has already followed the trailer, but whether the game can generate new content and new waves of attention that the market has not fully priced in once it reaches players.

If this fictional brand can continue attracting attention through GTA VI's global reach, DACITY could evolve from a rally driven by a single trailer into a Meme that the market trades repeatedly throughout the game's release cycle. This possibility has not yet been proven, but it is the core reason I believe this token is worth continuing to research.

author: eigencloud
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

quoted_text:
币安出了 AI Pro，我拿海力士试了试。

没让它预测涨跌，也没问“现在能不能买”。我给了它一个具体需求：能不能把海力士 ADR 和韩股之间的溢价，做成一个自动交易策略？

币安上这两个都有合约，SKHYUSDT 对应 ADR，SKHYNIXUSDT 对应韩国上市的海力士。

我的想法很简单：统一换股比例、汇率和合约单位后，ADR 溢价达到45%，就空 ADR、多韩股；溢价回到35%，两边一起平。

先不讨论这两个参数合不合理，也不是推荐大家照着做。我就是想看看，现在的交易所 AI，能把这件事做到哪一步。

聊下来，它确实懂我在说什么。

合约单位、换股比例、盘口深度、滑点、资金费，它都能列出来。甚至一边成交了、另一边没成交该怎么办，也会提醒你。

作为一个讨论策略的助手，我觉得是有用的。尤其是你脑子里只有一个大概想法的时候，跟它聊几轮，能把很多没想清楚的地方补上。

但我真正想要的，还在后面。

我问：那你能不能直接帮我做成 Bot，放在币安里运行，触发条件就交易？

它告诉我，目前不能在这里直接部署一个持续运行的 Bot，也不能替我自动启动实盘。

然后继续问我，要不要帮我写技术规格、设计回测框架。

看到这里，我的感觉是：方案聊得差不多了，接下来还是得我自己找人干活😂

当然，这里要说清楚。我截图里的入口显示的是“币安 AI”，官方对新版 AI Pro 的介绍里是有策略构建、模拟和实盘部署的。所以这次到底是入口没走对、功能还没开放到，还是不支持这种双腿策略，我还不能确定。

但一个普通用户用到这里，搞不清楚自己到底能不能做，其实也说明产品还有需要打磨的地方。

我最希望币安补上的，就是把这一步接起来。

比如我把海力士这个需求说完，它直接告诉我：

这两个合约能不能用，双腿策略支不支持，数据够不够。能做的话，生成一张策略图，把开仓、平仓、仓位和异常处理都摆出来，缺什么参数就继续问我。

然后先模拟跑着。

什么时候触发了，按当时盘口能不能成交，两边资金费一扣还剩多少，一腿没成交会怎么处理，都记下来给我看。

这些东西，比再给我一大段策略说明更有用。

交易的人应该都能理解，有时候你并不缺一个想法，缺的是把这个想法落地的时间和精力。

一个看起来很简单的价差策略，真要自己做，还得接行情、核对单位、写程序、找服务器、处理报错。做到一半，可能机会都过去了。

如果这些工作能在币安里面通过对话完成，我是愿意用的。

而且我对币安做这件事是有期待的。行情、账户、订单这些东西本来就在平台里，如果能接好，用户确实可以少折腾很多。

但这里最难的，可能也恰恰是后面这些事情。

解释为什么开仓，很容易。真遇到一边成交、一边卡住，怎么处理？策略暂停了，仓位还在不在？行情数据断了，是继续下单还是停下来？

真金白银跑起来，这些细节都得有交代。

我也不指望 AI 给我找个稳赚策略。45%的溢价可以变成55%，模拟赚钱也可以实盘亏钱。策略有没有优势，还是得自己研究。

我想交给它的，是那些已经想清楚、但自己懒得一遍遍盯着执行的规则。

这次体验，它帮我把问题梳理得更清楚了，但海力士这个 Bot 还没做出来。

后面如果能真正接上，我还会拿同一个例子继续试。

毕竟对我来说，判断这个产品好不好用，最后就看一件事：

我把需求说完之后，到底是多了一份说明书，还是多了一个能替我干活的工具。

quoted_text:
Counterintuitively crypto is good for this low liquidity environment because the space is so small in the grand scheme of things.

Despite money being tight at the moment, there exists an immense desire for retail traders to speculate, as we are in the later stages of a long cycle in risk appetite. Liquidity has a tendency to flow towards corners of the market where it can have an impact. There are fewer than 10 viable coins and it doesn't take much to move them.

In terms of the competing destinations for flows: gold has been challenged for a while now and AI is weighed down by concerns around financing availability and model-level pricing power.

It is hilarious and upside down that crypto would be the beneficiary of these conditions but it also makes sense in a strange way. At the end of the day, crypto is a tiny financial playground that is driven by the memetic consensus of a narrow group of people. In that sense it can transcend broader macro conditions.

author: 0xDeployer

text:
every wrap, unwrap, buy, and sell on a volatile log charges a fee (1% wrap/unwrap, 0.5% buy/sell; stable logs charge 0.2% wrap and 0.3% unwrap/buy/sell): 15% of each fee burns log tokens, 17% buys and burns CHOP, and 68% buys CHOP for staked lp farmers.

how the two numbers work:
- farmer apr: cumulative CHOP deposited for farmers (valued in the paired token at the current CHOP price) divided by the pool's current value (2x paired reserve), annualized since the log was created. farmers also earn the 0.3% v2 pool swap fee.
- backing apy: annualized growth of the underlying token per log token since creation, driven by the 15% log-token fee burn. plain chTOKEN holders earn this without farming.

what you can hypothetically earn:
- if you just hold a log token, your balance stays the same while the underlying tokens backing each chTOKEN grow as wrap, unwrap, and swap fees burn 15% of fees.
- if you farm (stake v2 lp), you earn a pro-rata share of the 68% fee stream paid out in CHOP plus the 0.3% v2 swap fee, while the chTOKEN half of your lp still accrues backing growth.
- at historical rates, a hypothetical deposit earns pro rata to your share of the staked pool — though because those pools can be small, adding fresh capital increases pool tvl and dilutes the apr on your own deposit unless fee volume scales up too.

both figures are backward-looking since creation, not a forecast, and fall when volume and volatility cool off. farming also carries impermanent loss between the log token and WETH, and wrapping/unwrapping costs fees so short round trips lose money, deployer.

author: pratikg
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

author: Xudong07452910
quoted_text:
The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. 

Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. 

When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. 

But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. 

Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

text:
하룻밤 사이에 반도체 투자심리가 갑자기 완전히 뒤바뀌었음.

어제까지만 해도 "미국 데이터센터 줄취소됐다, AI 거품 꺼진다"며 패닉에 빠졌던 시장에, 밤사이 일론 머스크의 스페이스X가 분위기를 단숨에 뒤집어버린 역대급 실적을 터뜨렸기 때문임.

1. "AI가 돈이 안 된다고? 우린 AI 매출 830% 폭증하고 흑자 전환했다"

- 그동안 반도체 주가를 억눌렀던 제일 큰 걱정이 "AI에 돈만 쏟아붓지 실제로 돈 버는 회사가 없다"는 거였음.

- 그런데 올해 초 AI 기업(xAI)을 합병한 스페이스X의 3분기 실적을 까보니, AI 부문 매출만 1년 전보다 무려 830% 폭증한 약 10.6조 원(75.6억 달러)을 찍음.

- 심지어 작년엔 2조 원 넘게 적자였던 AI 사업이 이번 분기엔 약 6,000억 원(4.31억 달러) '흑자'로 돌아서면서, 스페이스X 전체 분기 매출(약 20.4조 원)의 절반 이상을 AI가 벌어들이는 기염을 토함.

2. 딱 3개월(한 분기) 동안 설비투자에만 '27.4조 원'을 쏟아부음

- AI로 진짜 돈이 벌리니까 머스크가 데이터센터와 설비 늘리는 데 돈을 더 무섭게 퍼붓고 있음.

- 스페이스X가 이번 3분기 딱 3개월 동안 설비투자(Capex)에 쓴 돈만 무려 약 27.4조 원(196억 달러)으로, 1년 전(약 9.6조 원)보다 3배 가까이 폭증함.

- 돈 없는 중소 업체들이 데이터센터 취소한다고 시장은 덜덜 떨었는데, 정작 머스크 혼자서 한 분기에만 27조 원어치 투자를 지르고 있었던 거임. (같은 날 AI 서버 제조사 슈퍼마이크로도 예상치보다 최대 6조 원어치나 서버가 더 팔렸다고 깜짝 실적을 내며 시간외 주가가 11% 넘게 폭등함)

3. 결정타 — '테슬라 + 스페이스X 합병' 특별위원회 공식 가동

- 여기에 머스크가 실적 발표 자리에서 "테슬라와 스페이스X를 합병하기 위해 양사에 특별위원회를 꾸렸다"고 공식 발표함.

- 초지능 AI를 만드는 데 생각보다 훨씬 더 막대한 자원이 필요하다며, 테슬라(자율주행·로봇)와 스페이스X(우주·스타링크·xAI 데이터센터)의 자본과 AI 인프라를 아예 하나로 합치겠다는 초대형 승부수를 던진 거임.

최근 며칠 동안은 자금력이 부족한 중소 클라우드 업체들이 빚과 전력난을 못 버티고 데이터센터를 취소하니까, 시장도 "이제 AI 투자가 꺾여서 반도체도 끝났다"며 심리가 꺾였었음.

하지만 최대 고객사인 일론 머스크가 한 분기에만 27조 원을 쏟아붓고 테슬라·스페이스X 합병까지 꺼내 들면서, 초거대 데이터센터와 AI 인프라는 결국 돈 많은 소수 공룡 기업들만 감당할 수 있는 판이라는 게 확인됨. 중소 업체들은 나가떨어지더라도 공룡 기업들은 앞으로 더 공격적으로 투자하겠다는 의지가 뚜렷하게 보이면서 반도체 투자 심리도 같이 회복된 거임.

결국 최근 돌아가는 뉴스들을 하나로 묶어보면 앞으로 AI 판이 어떻게 나뉘어질지 어느정도 예측해볼 수 있음.

스페이스X·구글·아마존처럼 천문학적인 자본을 가진 공룡 기업들은 앞으로도 엔비디아 최상위 GPU와 초고가 HBM을 돈 걱정 없이 쓸어 담으며 초거대 데이터센터를 지을 거고,

grok 성능도 이에 따라 앞으로 프론티어 모델들과 비슷하거나 넘어서는 시기가 올 것으로도 보여짐.

반대로 자본이 부족하거나 규제를 받는 기업들은 어쩔 수 없이 앞서 다룬 뉴스들처럼 HBM 없이 저가형 메모리(LPDDR·GDDR7)나 소프트웨어 우회 기술로 살아남는 방법을 택할 수밖에 없음.

결국 앞으로 AI 산업은 자본력에 따라 기업 간, 그리고 국가 간 격차가 극단적으로 벌어질 수밖에 없고, 최상위 프론티어 AI 모델의 성능 역시 후발주자가 도저히 따라잡을 수 없을 만큼 큰 격차로 벌어지게 될 거임.

SpaceX三季度一跃成为新云领头羊，看凌晨spacex公布的最新三季度财报总营收同比增161%至近146亿美元，净利润44亿，分别较分析师预期高14%和134%。这份财报最突出的变化是，SpaceX的增长引擎已经从传统火箭发射和“星链”互联业务，进一步转向AI领域业务“超级智能”（SI）。详细说说：
1、AI业务
1）三季度AI收入75.6亿美元，环比增长195%，同比增长830%。盈利出现拐点，SI三季度运营利润4.31亿美元，而二季度仍亏损12.57亿美元，去年同期亏损17.22亿美元。若按公司口径，SI调整后EBITDA达到49.53亿美元，去年同期为亏损4.28亿美元；

3）SI解决方案与基础设施收入70.22亿美元，去年同期仅3.59亿美元；这基本上就是售卖云算力、API，当然云算力是大头。这个两级已远超CRWv、nbis，单看云算力营收规模已经能赶得上甲骨文了

AI业务从之前spacex的巨亏之源、已经成为了现金牛。

2、星链业务
1）星链互联收入52.48亿美元，环比增长22%，同比增长69%；运营利润23.67亿美元，同比增长99%；调整后EBITDA为34.99亿美元，同比增长82%。

2）核心是用户数量
三季度订阅用户1360万，二季度1200万，环比新增160万；
一季度1000万，去年同期720万。能看出来增速非常快。

3、航天业务
传统的航天（Space）业务三季度收入17.67亿美元，环比增长84%，同比增长6%，大致与分析师预期的约18亿美元业务收入一致。

当然也有两点注意的：
1）SpaceX三季度运营利润为27.91亿美元，但净利润达到44.04亿美元，高于运营利润本身。这说明净利润不仅来自主业改善，也受到非经营项目和税项的明显支撑（一次性的）

2）SpaceX三季度资本开支195.93亿美元，几乎与分析师预期的196亿美元一致，但绝对值极高，较当季营收高约34%，SI资本开支164.44亿美元，自由现金流为负。

text:
Biological intelligence to bootstrap robotic intelligence?

If robotics is about to enter its golden age, @MeckaAI is one of the companies feeding it, by sensorizing humans to train robots.

The biggest challenge robotics faces is the data flywheel cold start problem. LLMs got a free cold start from the internet: trillions of tokens, already written. Robotics gets nothing. Someone has to go create the training data to jumpstart the system.

@joshavata is the co-founder and CEO of Mecka, the data and deployment company for physical AI. Josh read every robotics paper he could find in late 2024, visited the labs, and made a bet: humans and humanoids look the same, so humans could act as the training fleet. Egocentric data, first-person video of people doing real work, could become vital fuel.

Two years ago, the biggest egocentric dataset was Ego4D at 4,000 hours. The field is now in the millions of hours, thanks in part to Mecka. We’re probably still orders of magnitude of training data away from robotics nirvana. But every rung on the physical intelligence ladder unlocks real commercial tasks. And eventually, Josh imagines a world with an order of magnitude more robots than people, of a plurality of shapes and sizes and use cases, as the Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy foretold :)

A few things we cover in this conversation.

- Why robotics has no cold start: pixels, actions and logic, and why pre-training data is a real market in robotics in a way it never was for LLMs

- What “teaching robots about carbon life” means: in sci-fi the final frontier is organic. The human brain runs on 20 watts and self-heals

- The egocentric bet: teleop couldn’t scale, humans and humanoids share a form, so Waymo-fy the humans. The first pilot was aunties and uncles recording themselves cooking on a mobile app

- Force data: video can’t tell a robot how hard to squeeze an egg. Wrist cameras are a hack. Mecka built the gloves instead

- Inside the data factory: a consumer app that streams your tasks, a B2B engine recruiting across “the taxonomy of all physical human work,” 100-gigabit upload lines, hundreds of petabytes

- Millions of hours vs. Tesla’s decade on two degrees of freedom, and why it’s a slow creep up, not a GPT-3 moment

- The home has the most data and is the hardest place to deploy. Laundry folding and assembly-line pick-and-place get solved in the next year or two

- Useful robots already exist: hotel delivery and cleaning bots in China and Southeast Asia, industrial cleaning in the US. Humanoids are the terminal state, not the first step

- Deployment diffusion: a modern systems integrator whose installed robot does something next week it couldn’t do last week. If Mecka ever helps deploy a robot that mines an asteroid, they’ve done their job

- The data pot of soup: a million hours of human data, tens of thousands of UMI, a few hours of in-domain teleop. Tactile and simulation haven’t entered the mix yet

- Move 37 for robotics: AlphaGo went behavior cloning, then self-play, then magic. The catch is the rules of the game are the entire physical world, and we don’t have the simulator yet

- Will the AGI labs steamroll robotics? “It takes a lot of courage to scale up data with imperfect information.”

- The Kawasaki Corleo, the robot panther-dog-horse on Mecka’s conference room wall, and why the future of robotics looks like Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy
