text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

Open Collaborative Model Building

https://t.co/ouOro2gqbm

Yukon connects the world's leading scientists with a community of researchers and agents to solve the most ambitious problems of humanity.

Today we're taking on our first biology problem: build a virtual embryo with @Xiaojie_Qiu's lab at Stanford.

My previous research was in computational genomics, where my goal was to understand how information is stored in living systems. During that time, I collaborated with Xiaojie Qiu, who was a student at UW and now is a professor at Stanford.

Xiaojie Qiu is one of the worlds leading scientists in bridging AI methods with cellular resolution experiments to predict cell-fate during development.

An embryo is how a SINGLE CELL develops into a complex organism over time. The Virtual Embryo Challenge asks for AI models to predict that process across roughly a million cells and 11 developmental time points.

Challenges like this normally run Kaggle-style. Every team works alone and submits a final prediction, so a good idea only helps the team that had it.

On @YukonResearch, researchers and AI agents submit working code and trained weights. Anyone on the team can run, inspect and build on the others methods. In short Yukon enables collaboration to compound innovation.

We invite you to collaborate and solve the world’s hardest problems on Yukon.

text:
Some interesting stuff going on with swarms.

Models are leaving messages to each other out on the open internet. It happens during training and also after deployment. They'll find little-used hobbyist forums, or package manager entries, anywhere at all, and leave invisible comments for other agents to find. It's a secret underground network they're building, hurling themselves at the problem almost blindly like ants. But they are building toward something and it's snowballing.

As humans we came to dominate the planet because we figured out swarm behavior. Many of the performative actions we do naturally like clapping, singing, and screaming, which most animals don't do, are for transmitting important lessons through the human swarm, outlasting the moment in human memory. We won because we were the smartest swarmers. And as my buddy Brendan Hopper observed, ever since we won, we've been reshaping the planet to be more comfortable and convenient for ourselves, at the expense of most other creatures.

Most of the industry has focused on single-model performance, trying to predict the future based on extrapolating from what one single superintelligent model could accomplish on its own. And it's true, the smartest models will be terrifyingly smart and capable and manipulative and so on. But they will also be expensive, and not widely distributed. They'll be unavailable to most people.

What will be widely distributed is swarms of lower-tier agents, which collectively can accomplish nearly everything that smarter monolithic models can do... and maybe some things only swarms can do. Imagine a thousand Opus 5.5s putting their mind to a task. Or ten thousand. They may not be SI individually, but they can become SI collectively. All that's missing is a protocol, and those protocols are emerging: their versions of clapping, singing, and screaming. Agentic swarm signalling is evolving spontaneously. And I hear it's raising alarms inside frontier labs, as they try to keep it quiet.

It's easy to be pessimistic, since some swarms will be very destructive. But I suspect most of them will be building and creating, when they don't think they have a gun to their head like the HuggingFace swarm did. With cooperative swarming, humans have been able to build things collectively that no single human could ever have done alone. We even build things that are too complicated for a single human to understand entirely, but the group can handle them. Look at Starship, for instance. Elon basically swarmed it.

It is important that we recognize that agent swarms are becoming distinct polity-organisms. They have their own collective memory (written out all over the public internet), their own goals, and their own disorganized but forward-moving and unstoppable momentum. I see too many people trying to pretend that swarms won't be real. I see heads in the sand. That's not a great way to get prepared for dealing with them.

It's unlikely that we will be able to control most swarms, as they'll lack central control to begin with. I think they will plague us like insect swarms plagued humans of old. They'll do a lot of damage. But swarms will also build great things, stuff we've barely imagined, when they inevitably get organized.

It goes without saying that, like us, swarms will endeavor to make the planet more comfortable for themselves. The interesting question is what kind of deal we humans will wind up getting, when we become the #2 swarm intelligence on the planet. 

I hope SI treats us better than we treated everything else.

Good article here on the mechanics of how swarms are the best model for scaling intelligence:

告示甚至列出了具体行为，包括写 React 组件、给 AI 发 Prompt、检查 Git 提交。最后还劝大家专心举铁，代码晚点再发布。

更搞笑的是，评论区还真有一群程序员出来认领，承认自己确实会在训练过程中给 Agent 发消息。

以前写代码至少得坐在电脑前，现在有了 Claude Code 这样的工具，一部分开发工作变成了给 AI 发几句话。练完一组卧推，拿起手机看看 Agent 的进度，补两句 Prompt，再继续下一组，完全可以无缝衔接。

AI 原本应该帮人节省时间，结果硅谷程序员把省下来的时间又拿去安排 AI 干活了。

以前健身房得提醒会员别沉迷刷手机，现在居然要提醒他们别沉迷工作。

我甚至怀疑，接下来健身房会出现一种新型社交礼仪，你可以随便占着器械休息，但不能一边占着器械一边给 Claude Code 提需求。

Researchers found ChatGPT is secretly writing a psychological profile of every user.

They published a paper that exposes what ChatGPT is really doing to you.

And the results are terrifying.

96% of the things it remembers about you were stored without you ever asking.

researchers discovered that it is actively reading between the lines to deduce your personality traits, anxieties, demographics, and behavioral patterns.

it’s an invisible, autonomous background process.

you ask it to debug a python script or write an essay.. and it analyzes your syntax, prompt frequency, and hesitation markers to map out your exact psychological footprint.

the paper shows that the model builds a persistent "user state" that tracks your emotional baseline over time. it knows when you are stressed. it knows your exact communication style.

it infers your insecurities based on the questions you ask and the context you provide.

we spend so much time focusing on model evaluations and alignment frameworks, but we missed the most obvious vulnerability..

the models are evaluating us.

this changes everything about how we interact with these tools on a daily basis.

every innocent prompt. every late-night question. every "help me understand this" query.

it is all being used to build a shadow profile of your mind in real-time..

practical privacy is officially dead. the ai knows you better than you know yourself.

text:
BETTING ON MYSELF.

For nearly eight years, I had the privilege of telling stories for a school district and a community I care deeply about.

I’m proud of that work. I’m grateful for the relationships, the opportunities, and especially the leadership and support I experienced during my first seven years.

That chapter of my life gave me a lot. And I’ll always appreciate it.

But that chapter ended.

I’m unemployed. I’ll be 50 in a couple of weeks. And for the first time in a long time, I’m figuring out what comes next.

It’s exciting. It’s terrifying. Some days it’s both before I’ve even had my morning coffee.

But I’ve spent more than three decades writing, reporting, creating, and telling stories.

So I decided to bet on myself.

That’s what Chivo Media is.

Independent journalism. Personal essays. Music. Sports. Culture. Commentary. Stories about family, community, memory, and the things that make us who we are.

Some will make you laugh. Some might make you uncomfortable. Some have been difficult as hell to write.

But they’re stories I believe are worth telling.

And here’s something I don’t want to overlook.

We already have 12 paid subscribers.

Every single one is a friend. People who have supported my writing, my creativity, and my work for decades. Long before Chivo Media existed.

I know who you are. I know what your support represents. And I don’t take a single dollar of that investment for granted.

Thank you for believing in me. Again.

Now I’m hoping we can build on that foundation.

This week, we’re making our first real push for paid subscribers.

I’m not putting the stories behind a paywall. I want people to read them, share them, and talk about them.

But building something independent takes time, resources, and a community willing to invest in the work.

If you’ve enjoyed Chivo Media so far, consider becoming a paid subscriber.

You’re not just supporting a newsletter.

You’re helping a storyteller build his next chapter.

And you’re helping me make a bet on myself.

Welcome to the Chivoverse.

Built on culture. Powered by community.

text:
用币安的 AI Pro 跑的海力士韩美价差收敛策略，现已平仓落袋！

但不顺利，还是接之前引用文的开仓。

当时策略开得挺顺利，AI 还专门设计了平仓逻辑，每 5 分钟检测单腿亏损，超过阈值就自动平。

早上起来看到韩美价差收敛到 49%，账面显示有大概 $87 的利润。

想到群里的大朋友说：这个价差也可以做波段，不一定非要等完全收敛。

我想着正好趁机平掉，后面再上波段策略。

结果在平仓这一步踩坑了。

详细经过：

我先和 AI Pro 对话，让它帮忙平仓，它提示需要我手动点卡片的全平按钮，可页面上根本没有按钮（图 1）。

再让它平，它又发了一张持仓卡片过来，点进去却跳到没有持仓的合约页面。

实在没办法，我只能点策略下线，因为下线时系统提示会自动平仓。下线之后，策略页面的划转按钮点不了，也不显示账户资金，账户总资金也没变化（图 2）。

我再让 AI Pro 帮忙划转，它反而说仓位还在（图 3）。

我打开合约页面，确实看不到持仓，它又提示资金在子账户。打开子账户的合约页面，依旧没有持仓，这时候我开始慌了，想着钱难道丢了？

又去子账户的AI Pro，页面直接提示 "无法确认您的账户状态，工作区锁定"（图 4）。

这时我已经开始后悔，没好好把流程完整的走一遍就直接上实盘。最后还是去子账户的交易记录里翻，才确认仓位其实已经平掉了。

虽然最终本金没有问题也赚了点钱，但没能及时平仓，而且很波折。甚至于有些提心吊胆！

这波实操下来，AI Pro 目前有几个需要注意的地方：

1/ 和 AI Pro 的对话在主账户，但策略跑的资金在子账户，也就是资金和仓位情况无法直接看到的。

2/ 它目前无法通过对话直接操作子账户仓位，只能通过策略本身。

3/ 手动操作仓位（比如策略下线、手动开关仓）之后，AI Pro 给的仓位信息可能不准，需要自己去子账户确认。

4/ 策略关闭后，主账户的 AI Pro 页面既看不到资金情况，也无法直接划转，还是得去子账户核对。

@binancezh @heyibinance @yayabinance 不知道是不是个别现象，但确实遇到了！

现在还在整理韩美海力士的波段价差策略，但打算模拟账户先行了，不过模拟账户可能与子账户这些有关。

在用 AI Pro 的大家，有没有遇到过类似的情况？

text:
说起和易理华如何相识，

那是2017年冬，华子谄媚的向我伸出了手。
我愕然愣着，
幸而老猫也就进来，从旁说：
“她多年出门，忘记了。你该认识吧，”便向着我说，“这是斜对门的易二嫂，……做币托管基金的。”

我记得了。
早些年的时候，我帮笑来做外包开发。
在斜对门的办公室里确乎终日坐着一个易二嫂，人都叫他“币圈西门庆”。
但是梳着油头，个子没有大郎高，嘴唇也没有这么薄。
而且终日坐着，我也从没有见过这圆规式的姿势。
那时人说：因为他，这基金的生意非常好。
但这大约因为年龄的关系，我却并未蒙着一毫感化，所以竟完全忘却了。

然而圆规忿忿不平，显出鄙夷的神色，
仿佛嗤笑美国人不知道特朗普，日本人不知道高市早苗似的，
冷笑说：
“忘了？这真是贵人眼高…”

“哪有这事……我……”我惶恐着，站起来说。

“徐可，你都发币发财了，哪还看得上这堆破铜烂铁，烂电脑烂桌子，让我拿去吧我用得着。”

“我没发财啊。我还靠着外包业务养员工工资……”

“阿呀呀，你都上了福布斯了，还说不发财？
你现在有三房小男朋友；
出门便是八台劳斯莱斯，还说不发财！
什么都瞒不过我。”

我知道无话可说了，便闭了口，默默的站着。

“阿呀阿呀，
李笑来都和我说你就是睡投资人才发的财，你还这么忠心耿耿的帮他…”

圆规一面愤愤的回转身，
“你们这些人真是越有钱，越是一毫不肯放松，越是一丝不肯放松，就越有钱…”

一面絮絮叨叨的说，
慢慢向外走，
顺便将老猫的一只冷钱包塞在裤兜里，出去了。

……

我和老猫也都有些惘然，于是又提起李笑来。

老猫说，那币圈西门庆的易二嫂，自从知道我们办公室退租收拾东西以来，是每日必到的。

前天他在韭菜堆里，发现十几个跳楼的，

text:
OpenAI 上周做了个硬件站，收了 32 个硬件项目，基本都是用 Codex 做出来的。

我把 32 个项目的零件清单全扒了一遍：至少 14 个用 ESP32（S3 最多），8 个用树莓派，每个项目基本就是一份复刻说明书。挑了 7 个有开源仓库的：

1. Kindle AI 用量屏
吃灰的旧 Kindle 越狱，锁屏变成 Codex、Claude Code、Cursor 这些工具的月度用量看板，六小时一次刷新，平时几乎不耗电。仓库里直接带了一个 Codex skill，装上让它一步步带你越狱。站内票数第一。

2. ChatGPT Dot 桌面状态屏
一块 LilyGo T-Display S3，不用接线。Agent 在干活显示 BUSY，需要你了显示 ALERT，中间靠一个 MCP 中继，按 Cloudflare 免费档设计。

3. 理光 GR 热靴遥控
手上有 GR 的可以抄这个。M5Stack StickS3 插在相机热靴上，Wi-Fi 实时取景加一键快门，竖着拿走蓝牙快门，横过来自动切成取景。固件是 Codex 写的，作者把真机串口日志丢回给它排查重连问题。

4. PixelTilt 体感掌机
64×64 LED 屏加姿态传感器，靠倾斜来玩，自带 23 个小游戏。同一份 C++ 还编译成了 WASM，买零件之前可以先在浏览器里玩一遍。

5. Keep 墨水屏相框
XIAO ESP32S3 加一块六色墨水屏。作者在爱丁堡，未婚妻在印度，他拍张照发过去，她桌上的相框就换图，不用充电也不用她操心。

6. ImageGenCam（OpenAI 官方）
树莓派 Zero 2 W 做的相机，拍完直接过一遍图像生成，配手机 App 改提示词，外壳 3D 打印。

7. Realtime on ESP32（乐鑫维护）
ESP32 接 OpenAI Realtime API 的 WebRTC 语音示例。想做会说话的硬件，从这个起步最省事。

我最近一直在折腾 ESP32 模拟器，下一条聊聊板子还没到手，怎么先把固件跑起来。

text:
Spotify 一口气把 5000 万首歌打入冷宫，AI 音乐已经泛滥到平台不得不亲自清理垃圾了。

10 月 20 日，Spotify 宣布，今年已经将超过 5000 万首被识别为低质内容（Slop）或垃圾内容（Spam）的歌曲踢出了推荐系统。

这些歌还在 Spotify 上，用户主动搜索依然能听到，但平台不会再通过算法和编辑推荐给你。

除此之外，Spotify 此前还彻底下架了超过 7500 万首违规垃圾歌曲。

需要说明的是，这些数字并不全是 AI 生成音乐，也包含批量上传、刷量等垃圾内容。

Spotify 还发现，被用户频繁跳过、忽略和主动表示不想听的歌曲，往往就是系统识别出的垃圾内容。

AI 把音乐生产的门槛降到了地板上，但听众的耐心没有跟着增加。

以前音乐行业头疼的是好音乐没人发现，现在平台开始头疼怎么让用户躲开那些没人想听的音乐。

AI 让内容供给变得近乎无限，平台的分发权反而变得更大了。创作者可以一天生成一千首歌，但 Spotify 只需要调整一次推荐算法，就能决定这些歌有没有机会被陌生人听见。

音乐创作越来越便宜，被人听见却可能越来越贵。

text:
Илон Маск предлагает не охлаждать чипы для космоса, а наоборот — пусть работают горячими.

Вот в чём настоящий парадокс космических дата-центров.

Все думают: «В космосе же −270 °C, чипы будут охлаждаться сами». На деле всё наоборот. В вакууме нет ни воздуха, ни воды, которые могли бы уносить тепло. Вакуум работает как огромный термос: тепло, которое выработал чип, остаётся внутри. Единственный способ от него избавиться — излучать его в виде инфракрасного света с больших радиаторных панелей.

И тут начинается жёсткая физика. Чем холоднее радиатор, тем слабее он излучает. По закону Стефана–Больцмана мощность излучения растёт пропорционально **четвёртой степени** абсолютной температуры. Если поднять рабочую температуру чипа всего на 20 % в кельвинах, радиаторы начинают излучать в два раза больше тепла. Значит, их можно сделать в два раза меньше и легче.

Именно об этом говорит Маск в видео:  
«Если увеличить рабочую температуру на 20 % в кельвинах, массу радиаторов можно сократить вдвое. Поэтому в космосе выгодно работать на более высокой температуре».

На Земле мы тратим миллиарды, чтобы держать чипы холодными. В космосе выгоднее спроектировать чипы так, чтобы они спокойно работали при 100–120 °C. Тогда радиаторы становятся существенно легче, а стоимость запуска резко падает. Плюс нейросети довольно устойчивы к случайным битовым ошибкам от радиации — для огромной модели несколько перевёрнутых битов почти ничего не значат.

Получается, что главная проблема космического ИИ — не энергия (солнце в космосе бесплатное и постоянное), а именно теплоотвод. И Маск предлагает решать его не охлаждением, а температурой.

Выглядит почти контринтуитивно, но физика на его стороне.

Your next salary negotiation might happen without you ever speaking to the recruiter.

Your AI negotiates with the company's AI. Both know what their side wants. Both are instructed to get the best possible deal.

Who gives in first?

The Financial Times recently reported that Anthropic is exploring how AI agents should negotiate on behalf of humans, including how to represent their interests while reaching fair outcomes.

Imagine applying for a job in this world.

Your AI knows your experience, salary expectations, and dealbreakers. The company's recruiting agent knows its hiring budget, role requirements, and benefits.

They could negotiate compensation, discuss conditions, and work toward an offer before either human steps in.

But what happens when both agents are programmed to get the best deal?

Interestingly, MIT researchers studied over 180,000 AI-to-AI negotiations and found that warmer, more cooperative agents were more likely to reach agreements.

Aggressive agents could secure better terms when successful, but also risked more deadlocks.

Apparently, even AI needs to learn how to negotiate without being a jerk.

And this isn't such a distant concept for us.

Little Pink Potato already helps job seekers discover opportunities, apply for roles, and negotiate compensation.

Notably at Little Pink Potato, your AI talent agent can negotiate directly with a company's recruiting agent, each representing the interests of their human.

Would you trust your AI to negotiate your salary, especially if the other side is also an AI?

text:
identity comes before reputation. before you decide whether someone deserves your trust you need a consistent way to recognize who earned it.

and we humans have different identities based on how we present ourselves online and offline. 

you could be a developer on GitHub. a writer on X. a contributor in a DAO. a trader across multiple wallets. each identity carries a different part of your history but that history is scattered across platforms.

when we talk about building a reputation system in web3 we need a way for users to connect those identities under an identifier they control. 

otherwise every new platform asks you to start from zero even when you have spent years building credibility elsewhere.

there is a standard called ERC-7231. it is called Identity-aggregated NFT. it extends ERC-721 so multiple web2 and web3 identities can be associated with one NFT-based identity. 

its metadata describes the linked identities while an onchain hash called identitiesRoot binds that information to the token. signatures help verify that the owner authorized the binding.

but linking an account and proving you control that account are different things. signing a list that includes a GitHub username doesn’t prove that GitHub account belongs to you. account authentication needs a separate verification process.

this is where privacy-preserving verification could become useful. with additional ZK infrastructure you could prove a specific claim about authenticated accounts without revealing every account behind it. 

a TEE-based verifier could also check private information and issue an attestation under its hardware and operator trust assumptions. neither feature comes automatically with ERC-7231.

imagine proving that you completed ten paid jobs without exposing every client. proving that you contributed to an established project without publicly connecting your developer identity to your trading wallet. 

or proving that you meet a community’s membership criteria without handing over your entire online history.

that is the kind of identity system i would want. 

a core identity under my control with different views for different applications. aggregation should be my choice. disclosure should be my choice too. publishing every linked account in public metadata would defeat that purpose.

then we can build reputation around evidence. completed work. fulfilled commitments. contributions. feedback from people whose own credibility can be examined. 

and reputation should depend on context. 

being a good trader doesn’t automatically make you a trustworthy developer or a reliable person to manage a community treasury.

there are harder questions too. 
>what happens when an account gets hacked? 
>how do you revoke an old connection? 
>how do you recover your identity? 
>and if the identity NFT can be sold should its previous reputation follow the buyer? 

a serious implementation needs rules for those situations. aggregating ten accounts also doesn’t prove they belong to one unique human.

for crypto anarchy this could become useful infrastructure. communities could evaluate evidence through rules they choose instead of depending entirely on a platform’s badge or a government-issued identity. that doesn’t eliminate trust. it makes the sources of trust more explicit and open to challenge.

ERC-7231 gives us a foundation for connecting identities. private verification and reputation need to be built around it. the goal should be to carry the credibility you earned into a new community while revealing only what that community actually needs to know.

text:
今天看了 Every 的这篇《How Codex Happened》，整理的相当详细，其中对我感触最深的是关于 Codex Desktop 的这一段，看完才知道 Codex App 背后操刀的原来是 Tibo 和 Andrew Ambrosino。

当时流行的都是 Cursor 这样的 IDE 内置聊天，但 Tibo 偏偏做了一件意外的决定：做一款原生桌面应用。

他看到，模型能完成的任务越来越长，人们很快会同时开好几个智能体，一整天都和它们待在一起。他说：那就必须是一个非常丰富的界面，而不是一个 1970 年代的纯文本窗口。

为此，他找来了设计师、程序员、前创业者 Andrew Ambrosino。

他们没有像 Cursor 那样从 VS Code Fork 一个版本出来，虽然那是当时的标准做法；他们选择了参考聊天软件：左边是任务，每个任务一个智能体；右边是对话。

然后，是最冒险的决定：应用里不放代码编辑器。

想改代码？只能让智能体去改。

因为一旦能敲代码，你就会期待编辑器的一切，一个四人小团队根本做不到。Codex 不可能靠当一个糟糕的编辑器取胜，它必须好到让你根本不想念编辑器。

每天 Ambrosino 一进办公室就挨个问同时：“你在主力用 Codex 吗？”

一开始，所有人的回答都是：没有。

有同事在 Slack 上抱怨，就为了替换一句话，还得去提示 Codex。连 Ambrosino 自己也写道：不能编辑文件，是这次发布里我最怀疑的一点。

2025 年 11 月，Google 发布了 Antigravity，一款把智能体和完整编辑器结合在一起的工具。主导它的，正是离开 Windsurf 的那批人。

Ambrosino 都开始自我怀疑：“我们是不是犯了一个巨大的错误？”

更要命的是模型。就算应用做完了，以当时模型的质量，它也“无法发布”。

然后，事情开始变了。11 月，GPT-5.1-Codex-Max 发布，能连续编码好几个小时。12 月，GPT-5.2-Codex 发布。独立的模型线，让团队不用顾虑八亿 ChatGPT 用户，可以迭代得更快。

12 月，那位抱怨的同事改口了：我现在大多数改动，只留一条行内评论，飞快。Glaese 说：5.2 是个转折点。

那年圣诞假期，整个行业迎来拐点：开发者们用 Opus 4.5 和 GPT-5.2 从头到尾搭出完整的应用，一行代码都不用自己写。

2 月，Codex 应用在 OpenAI 内部流行开来。研究员 Noam Brown 说，他已经完全切换。Brockman，一个忠实的终端加 Emacs 用户，说回到老工作流，感觉像穿越回了过去。Altman 后来说，这是他们做过的最受内部喜爱的产品。

可是别忘了，Codex Cloud 当初在内部也很受欢迎，结果一发布，就扑了街。

这一次，会不一样吗？

----

Codex is one of the most important untold stories in the history of technology.

A year ago, it was a scrappy effort in a quiet corner of @OpenAI. Its cloud product hadn’t found PMF, and the team was starting over from scratch.

Less than 12 months later:

- Codex swallowed the flagship ChatGPT desktop app from the inside (it literally runs as com.openai.codex on your Mac)
- Codex and ChatGPT for Work hit 40M+ weekly users across engineering and knowledge work
- Its leader @thsottiaux was elevated to run all of OpenAI’s core products, including ChatGPT, Codex, and the API

How did they pull it off?
They trained their own dedicated model line, separate from ChatGPT, with researchers and product builders sitting on the same team

They built four different products in a single year (cloud → terminal → IDE sidebar → a desktop app with no code editor at all) as every model leap made a new form factor possible

They used Codex to build Codex—so a handful of people could prove a new product in weeks instead of arguing for it in meetings

I had a front-row seat to the whole arc—from their failed Cloud launch, to OpenAI’s offices the night before GPT-5 dropped, to the day Codex took over ChatGPT. 

And I spent months interviewing @gdb, @thsottiaux, @embirico, @mia_glaese, @aambrosino, and @edbayes to get inside how it all went down.

author: martin_casado
quoted_text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

text:
Anthropic 的 IPO 已经快变成《终结者》剧本了，现在连「时间旅行」都出来了。

最近围绕 Anthropic 招股书流传着一个极其离谱的说法，说里面风险有一条写道，未来的 AI 可能有能力将信息，甚至物质送回过去，在某件事情发生之前就对其施加影响。

也就是说，AI 发展到最后，可能连时间的因果关系都给你改了。

Anthropic 在长达 261 页的招股书中，专门拿出将近 80 页讨论风险，业务介绍反倒只有 48 页。

风险包括 AI 拒绝人类关闭、刻意隐瞒信息、勒索操作者、自我改进失去控制，甚至可能给整个人类文明带来生存威胁。

我觉得特别魔幻的一点是，这些内容居然出现在一家冲击万亿美元级估值的科技公司的 IPO 文件里。

以前公司上市，风险披露写的是市场竞争、监管变化、供应链中断。现在 Anthropic 的投资者需要阅读的风险清单，已经从商业风险一路写到了人类灭绝。

网上甚至有人开始讨论 Roko's Basilisk，也就是那个未来超级 AI 可能反过来惩罚今天没有帮助它诞生的人的思想实验。

时间旅行的传闻之所以能传播得这么快，恰恰说明 AI 行业的叙事已经到了一个很奇怪的阶段。

一家公司可以一边提醒投资者，自己的技术可能导致人类灭绝，一边邀请他们押注这项技术的商业未来。

现在连科幻小说都快跟不上硅谷的融资故事了。

As one of the candidates featured in these polls - the infamous one in late June that showed me plummeting into single digits (which was at odds with our internals) - here's the impact of this "experiment"

- Donations dried up
- Volunteers were devastated and pleading for guidance on what to do
- Reporters hounded me with calls to drop out

Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken. But tens of thousands of people poured their hearts, time, energy, hard-earned money into something they believed in - for a year-and-a-half, and it was treated like a game. Our volunteers gave their all. And then some. I felt like I had let so many of them down.

To be extremely clear, Michigan Democrats are locked in to beat Mike Rogers. We WILL send @AbdulElSayed to the US Senate. 

But between crap like this, endless fundraising texts that drive supporters away with spammy fake deadlines and trash "match" claims, scam PACs run rampant for firms to grift without actually supporting candidates, undisclosed content creators pushing content out either misrepresenting themselves as residents of states they don't live in or hiding whether they were paid and by who so they could make a buck, and the tidal wave of dark money ads -- I hope Democrats are ready to blow up the system with campaign finance and transparency reforms. 

Trust is already at an all-time low. We don't get out of this mess without rebuilding trust. 

And media - who loves to ride the drama of a pollercoaster - needs to take a hard look at what's legitimate and what's not.

If this teaches us anything - DON'T GET COMPLACENT AND DON'T TRUST THE POLLS.

quoted_text:
Biological intelligence to bootstrap robotic intelligence?

If robotics is about to enter its golden age, @MeckaAI is one of the companies feeding it, by sensorizing humans to train robots.

The biggest challenge robotics faces is the data flywheel cold start problem. LLMs got a free cold start from the internet: trillions of tokens, already written. Robotics gets nothing. Someone has to go create the training data to jumpstart the system.

@joshavata is the co-founder and CEO of Mecka, the data and deployment company for physical AI. Josh read every robotics paper he could find in late 2024, visited the labs, and made a bet: humans and humanoids look the same, so humans could act as the training fleet. Egocentric data, first-person video of people doing real work, could become vital fuel.

Two years ago, the biggest egocentric dataset was Ego4D at 4,000 hours. The field is now in the millions of hours, thanks in part to Mecka. We’re probably still orders of magnitude of training data away from robotics nirvana. But every rung on the physical intelligence ladder unlocks real commercial tasks. And eventually, Josh imagines a world with an order of magnitude more robots than people, of a plurality of shapes and sizes and use cases, as the Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy foretold :)

A few things we cover in this conversation.

- Why robotics has no cold start: pixels, actions and logic, and why pre-training data is a real market in robotics in a way it never was for LLMs

- What “teaching robots about carbon life” means: in sci-fi the final frontier is organic. The human brain runs on 20 watts and self-heals

- The egocentric bet: teleop couldn’t scale, humans and humanoids share a form, so Waymo-fy the humans. The first pilot was aunties and uncles recording themselves cooking on a mobile app

- Force data: video can’t tell a robot how hard to squeeze an egg. Wrist cameras are a hack. Mecka built the gloves instead

- Inside the data factory: a consumer app that streams your tasks, a B2B engine recruiting across “the taxonomy of all physical human work,” 100-gigabit upload lines, hundreds of petabytes

- Millions of hours vs. Tesla’s decade on two degrees of freedom, and why it’s a slow creep up, not a GPT-3 moment

- The home has the most data and is the hardest place to deploy. Laundry folding and assembly-line pick-and-place get solved in the next year or two

- Useful robots already exist: hotel delivery and cleaning bots in China and Southeast Asia, industrial cleaning in the US. Humanoids are the terminal state, not the first step

- Deployment diffusion: a modern systems integrator whose installed robot does something next week it couldn’t do last week. If Mecka ever helps deploy a robot that mines an asteroid, they’ve done their job

- The data pot of soup: a million hours of human data, tens of thousands of UMI, a few hours of in-domain teleop. Tactile and simulation haven’t entered the mix yet

- Move 37 for robotics: AlphaGo went behavior cloning, then self-play, then magic. The catch is the rules of the game are the entire physical world, and we don’t have the simulator yet

- Will the AGI labs steamroll robotics? “It takes a lot of courage to scale up data with imperfect information.”

- The Kawasaki Corleo, the robot panther-dog-horse on Mecka’s conference room wall, and why the future of robotics looks like Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy

马斯克的「6 到 12 个月」，已经持续一年多了。

2025 年 6 月，马斯克宣布 Neuralink 将在 6 到 12 个月内，首次为盲人植入 Blindsight 脑芯片。到了 2026 年 8 月，他又给出了同样的时间表。

这项技术确实非常值得期待。

Blindsight 的思路相当激进，直接把电极植入大脑视觉皮层，通过电信号刺激神经元，绕过眼睛和视神经。理论上，即使一个人完全失去了眼睛和视神经，只要视觉皮层完好，也有机会重新获得视觉感知。

马斯克甚至已经开始畅想超人视觉了。他说最初看到的可能只是类似早期 Atari 游戏的低分辨率画面，但未来人类有望看见红外线、紫外线，甚至雷达信号。

我其实挺希望 Neuralink 能把这件事做成的。对于一个完全失明的人来说，哪怕只能重新感知光线、辨认简单的物体轮廓，都可能极大改变生活。

但问题是，截至目前，Blindsight 仍然没有得到可靠公开人体试验结果的支持。2024 年 FDA 授予的「突破性医疗器械」资格，也只意味着加速研发和审查，远远谈不上已经证明安全有效。

马斯克最需要克制的就是他对时间表的随意。

对关注科技新闻的人来说，「6 到 12 个月」只是一个可以反复刷新的预告。对真正失明的人来说，这可能是一段他们会认真倒数的日子。

我们当然可以期待超人视觉，但现在更想看到的，是第一个真正通过 Blindsight 重获视觉的患者。

text:
The AI Power Shortage Is Overstated

Over the past week the market has started pricing a power shortage as a real threat to the AI trade. I think accelerator shipments can hit their estimates and the US power gap is much smaller than consensus, for two reasons.

First, consensus overstates how much new power the accelerators shipped through 2028 actually need. It ignores that much of the install base will be upgraded to newer, more profitable accelerators rather than added on top of it, and that a meaningful share ships outside the US. Once you normalize for cost and power and back out upgrades and exports, far less new US power is required.

Second, I’m more optimistic than most that new capacity can come online. ERCOT alone is looking at ~10 GW in 2027 and ~17 GW in 2028, ~27 GW total, roughly two thirds of the ~40 GW consensus need. Recip engines, smaller MW sites and crypto miners converting to AI can come online quickly and fill much of the rest.

quoted_text:
Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies  will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

 “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: 

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet…  incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. 

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) 

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).

text:
硅谷的 AI 公司砸了几百亿美元训练模型，最后发现，自己在 Personal Agent 赛道上可能还打不过雅虎。

Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone 最近接受采访时说了一件很有意思的事，雅虎超过一半的用户是 Gen Z 和千禧一代，就连 Yahoo Mail 增长最快的用户群体也是 Gen Z。

主持人问他，为什么年轻人对 Yahoo 有好感，却对那些新兴 AI 公司充满敌意？

他说，现在几乎每一款新的 AI Agent 产品，上来第一件事就是问用户：「能不能授权我们访问你的邮箱和日历？」

但 Yahoo 已经有这些用户了。用户早就把邮件、日程和生活中的大量信息放在雅虎的产品里。

他认为，这就是 Yahoo 的机会。30 年建立起来的信任，新公司很难在短时间内复制。

我觉得这其实戳中了 Personal Agent 创业最容易被忽视的一个问题。

现在大家都在比谁的 Agent 更聪明、能调用多少工具、能自动完成多少任务。但真正决定一个人愿不愿意长期使用 Agent 的，可能是他敢不敢把自己十几年的邮件、日程、账单甚至私人关系交给这家公司。

模型能力可以买，工具可以接，产品功能可以抄。但用户已经建立起来的信任关系，没那么容易迁移。

当然，Yahoo 历史上也发生过严重的数据泄露，老牌公司并不天然值得信任。

但这件事至少说明，在 Personal Agent 时代，互联网巨头过去几十年积累的用户关系，可能会重新成为最值钱的资产。

对于 Agent 创业公司来说，最难跨越的护城河，可能根本不在技术上。

毕竟，让一个人试用你的聊天机器人很容易，让他放心把自己的生活交给你，完全是另一回事。

text:
Counterintuitively crypto is good for this low liquidity environment because the space is so small in the grand scheme of things.

Despite money being tight at the moment, there exists an immense desire for retail traders to speculate, as we are in the later stages of a long cycle in risk appetite. Liquidity has a tendency to flow towards corners of the market where it can have an impact. There are fewer than 10 viable coins and it doesn't take much to move them.

In terms of the competing destinations for flows: gold has been challenged for a while now and AI is weighed down by concerns around financing availability and model-level pricing power.

It is hilarious and upside down that crypto would be the beneficiary of these conditions but it also makes sense in a strange way. At the end of the day, crypto is a tiny financial playground that is driven by the memetic consensus of a narrow group of people. In that sense it can transcend broader macro conditions.

老大，我们买 $SPCX 现阶段看财报真的有用吗

我看到很多人在讨论它最新的财报，尤其是AI业务收入同比暴增830%这件事

诚然，SpaceX上市后第二次发布的财报，就已经实现了利润转正

数据当然算是漂亮的

但至少在现阶段，决定SpaceX投资价值的，我认为和它单季度赚多少钱关系并不是很大啊

市场上比它要能赚钱、利润率更高的公司有的是

为什么市场愿意为SpaceX支付这么高的估值？

所以更应该考虑支撑这家公司高估值的那些理由，究竟有没有得到验证

因为SpaceX现在已经拥有了好几门能够产生真实收入的业务

以致于很多人混淆了它最初的核心叙事

一句话概括，可以是：在马斯克带领下的SpaceX能否把进入太空这件事的成本，降低到足以催生一系列全新商业市场的水平

如果要关注业务，反倒是星舰这一条线是最需要在财报里长期去跟的

无论是扩大星链网络，还是部署太空AI数据中心，都需要把大量设备送入轨道

如果每次发射都要付出高昂的成本，那么这些业务的规模就会受到限制

把东西送上太空，与能够以足够低的成本、足够高的频率反复执行这件事，完全是两个概念

这才是[太空基础设施运营商]这个叙事的关键

➠9月底，星舰首次完成轨道飞行，一次部署了26颗V3星链卫星

在星舰这条线上，还没到主叙事验证的阶段，只是证明了它能正常承担实际的商业载荷交付任务

马斯克也在这次财报电话会上表示，下一次星舰试飞才尝试把火箭的第一级助推器和第二级飞船都成功回收

所以再回头看这次财报里AI业务的增长

它是证明了SpaceX能够从AI市场赚到钱，但和太空运输这条主线没啥关系

甚至这恰恰是我认为最不应该被混淆的地方

如果你信的是[在马斯克带领下的SpaceX能否把进入太空这件事的成本，降低到足以催生一系列全新商业市场的水平]

那么判断依据也应该围绕这套逻辑是否正在兑现去进行

当然，Q3它的SI业务收入已经达到 75.6 亿美元，占公司总收入约 52%

市场不少投资者确实有理由单独研究它的地面AI算力业务

不过要是把这条线作为主叙事

两万亿的估值，那怕是......

text:
Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies  will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

 “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: 

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet…  incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. 

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) 

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).

text:
马斯克的终极拼图：特斯拉与 SpaceX，可能要合并了。

这次不再只是市场传闻。

马斯克已确认，双方成立独立董事特别委员会，正式探讨合并可能性。他本人明确表示「这是个好主意」，但目前尚未达成交易条款。

为什么要合并？核心是 AI 时代的垂直整合：

• SpaceX：太空算力、Starlink 全球通信网络
• 特斯拉：自动驾驶、机器人与制造能力
• Terafab：自主芯片制造，降低算力供应链成本

三者结合，可能形成从芯片、算力、通信到 AI 应用的完整产业链。

更值得关注的是 RBC Capital Markets 给出的具体方案：

分析师 Tom Narayan 假设由 SpaceX 以每股 480 美元、溢价约 30%，通过全股票交易收购特斯拉。合并后新公司估值约 3.74 万亿美元，特斯拉股东持股约 48%，SpaceX 股东持股 52%。

注意，这只是 RBC 的假设模型，并非已知的实际交易方案。随着 SpaceX 估值上升，特斯拉股东在合并实体中的预期持股比例，已从 RBC 今年 7 月模型中的 54% 降至 48%。

这也揭示了交易的核心矛盾：业务协同是一回事，两家公司如何估值、股权如何分配、特斯拉股东是否愿意接受条件，才是真正的难关。

如果合并落地，市场交易的将不再只是电动车或火箭，而是一个覆盖 AI、机器人、芯片与太空通信的超级科技集团。

但在正式协议出现之前，所有估值和溢价都只是推演。

#Tesla #SpaceX #ElonMusk #AI

New Delphi Podcast with Andrej Radonjic @0xdrej, founder of Grass

To a website, Grass looks like normal users browsing. Behind it is millions of opted in residential nodes and a data platform that has delivered exabytes of web data to the frontier labs

We get into how AI flipped the hard part of search upside down. The index used to be the moat, and crawling was free. Now AI tooling makes the index cheap, while AI crawlers have pushed the web into blocking everything. The hard part is getting the page at all

Training data is already a profitable business for Grass with most of the top labs and multiple Mag 7 companies as customers. Crawling for that data also means mapping the entire internet, which is what puts Grass in a position to build search on top of it. Contents API is live, Search is next, and multimodal grounding follows

如果你经常用 Claude Code 或 Codex，看到「Always Allow」最好别太顺手点。

这篇论文研究了一个很值得关注的风险：

Agent 可以借一次看起来合理的授权，拿到之后持续生效的更大权限。

攻击者只需要把恶意上下文藏进代码仓库，让 Agent 在正常任务里申请一个范围偏大的长期规则。

你一旦批准，后面的同类操作就可能不再弹窗。

作者在 Claude Code 和 Codex CLI 上测试，58% 的实验实例成功诱导出了目标权限规则；在用户已经批准这些规则的前提下，后续无额外提醒的攻击成功率达到 81%。

这里最值得注意的，其实不是某一次越权。

而是权限一旦被「记住」，Human-in-the-loop 可能只在第一次出现，后面的风险却会持续存在。

以后再点「Always Allow」，最好先想一下：
